declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of dQuant Capital Management, an investment firm that utilizes quantitative strategies. The theoretical framework presented in this paper, including the Aggregate Perceived Risk (APR) model, informs the proprietary methodologies used by the firm. No external funding was received for this research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was independently funded by the author and dQuant Capital Management.

detail.abstract: The Aggregate Perceived Risk (APR) framework introduces a unified, non-linear pricing equation where market value reflects the geometric interaction of fundamental value, a capital-weighted perception denominator, and a structural exponent capturing institutional frictions. This endogenizes volatility clustering, discontinuities, and regime shifts. The paper delivers five results. It formalizes a single valuation operator integrating fundamentals, perception, and structural constraints. It builds a derivative-based alpha framework that identifies perceptual exhaustion and the inflection points where Perception Gap velocity eliminates contrarian timing risk. It shows heavy tails and endogenous jumps arise directly from perception dynamics without external shocks. It resolves the parameter paradox by proving structural tightening becomes expansionary in hyper-complacent regimes through a sign inversion in. And it establishes a microstructural mechanism for ∂𝑃 ∂𝑘 bubbles and crashes, where rapid shifts in aggregate perception create velocity mismatches that overpower fundamentals. APR thus provides a compact architecture linking behavioral dynamics, institutional constraints, and nonlinear price formation within one mathematical specification.

title: Platform Power in News Aggregation
affiliations: Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Stanford, Universitat Pompeu Fabra and Universitat Pompeu Fabra (UPF)

detail.title: Platform Power in News Aggregation
detail.abstract: News aggregators are among the primary gatekeepers of online news, shaping both consumption and production through the algorithms that rank stories and sources. We provide the first large-scale estimates of this algorithmic power using the example of Yandex News, Russia's largest aggregator. Combining archived front pages with 12.3 million published articles and outlet-level traffic data, we estimate that occupying the entire top-5 news block for a day raises an outlet's traffic by roughly 380,000 visitors. After a 2016 law made aggregators liable for cited content, Yandex halved its references to independent outlets, yet consumers did not penalize the manipulation: its referrals converted readers at the same rate, and its market share did not fall. Removed outlets shifted toward longer articles and stopped optimizing headlines for the algorithm, showing that aggregator algorithms shape not only news consumption but also production.

title: The Economics of Menstrual Health: State of the Art and Descriptive Evidence
affiliations: University of Bordeaux

detail.title: The Economics of Menstrual Health: State of the Art and Descriptive Evidence
detail.abstract: Across the European Union, the tax on menstrual products is being cut and free-provision schemes are spreading, yet the evidence guiding these decisions is thin and largely imported from low-income settings. This paper asks what is actually known about the economics of menstruation, and what a policymaker still cannot answer. Reading economics alongside public health and medicine, it finds a recurring pattern: the outcomes that respond to policy, product use, comfort, and well-being, are rarely the ones on which policy is justified, while the headline claims that are, that menstruation drives cyclical absenteeism, or that a tax cut mechanically reaches consumers, turn out to be fragile or unverified beyond a single case. The paper then assembles the descriptive evidence Europe lacks. Across 24 member states, a year of menstrual products costs between 0.23 and 1.12 percent of the national poverty line, or 3.9 to 16.2 hours of minimum-wage work: a burden set by income, not price, and near-invisible at median income. Some 94 million women are affected, spending on the order of 5.3 billion euros a year. Mapping the two instruments under debate, the VAT schedule and free provision, it also gives the first tabulation of exactly which products each European reform covers, showing that Germany, the most-studied case, is the only one to leave a mainstream product taxed. What this leaves open defines an agenda for causal work.

title: When AI Hides the Source: A Game-Theoretical Analysis of Open-Source Disclosure
affiliations: Fudan and Fudan University - School of Management

detail.title: When AI Hides the Source: A Game-Theoretical Analysis of Open-Source Disclosure
detail.abstract: Generative AI tools can transform software artifacts so extensively that downstream use remains technically valuable while the connection to the source becomes difficult to verify. This creates a governance problem that conventional software-provenance systems do not fully address: they can authenticate a project's declared repository and build process, but they cannot establish that the declared history includes every contributing predecessor. We develop a game-theoretic model in which an original project chooses how much reusable knowledge to disclose and a later project decides whether to credit the source or claim independent origin. When the originator's return from openness depends strongly on visible credit, it limits sharing to the maximum safe disclosure-the largest amount that does not induce a false origin claim-and may close entirely. When broad use remains valuable without credit, the originator can remain open at a lower disclosure level even as reuse is concealed. We then study a governance rule that combines a signed origin claim, independent records, and a bounded penalty. Evidence and penalties reinforce one another, and AI creates a countervailing effect: it reduces disclosure by weakening code-based detection, yet can raise the marginal value of process records that do not rely on final-code similarity. Incomplete or overlapping records, limited penalties, and insufficient platform investment create a governance ceiling. Our results also show how protecting visible lineage can sustain voluntary disclosure in open-source ecosystems.

title: Shelter, Wealth and Affordability Canada's Real Estate Market in a Repriced Global Economy: Real Value, Household Debt, Supply, International Models and Scenarios
affiliations: Szymon Zephan Capital (SZC Group)

detail.title: Shelter, Wealth and Affordability Canada's Real Estate Market in a Repriced Global Economy: Real Value, Household Debt, Supply, International Models and Scenarios

declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: SZC Group

detail.abstract: This paper examines Canada's housing market within the post-pandemic repricing of global residential real estate. It distinguishes nominal home prices from real value after inflation, income, rent, financing, insurance, tax and maintenance costs. Canada entered 2026 with prices below their 2022 peak, affordability still impaired, household credit-market debt near $1.80 per dollar of disposable income, and a construction pipeline that risked weakening before the structural supply gap had closed. The analysis traces Canada's housing eras, the pandemic demand shock, material and labour disruptions, rapid population growth and subsequent moderation, regional divergence, mortgage renewal risk, climate insurance, political economy and geopolitical transmission. International cases show that no single model solves the problem: Singapore combines public land, subsidized ownership and macroprudential controls; Vienna preserves a large permanently affordable rental stock; Auckland demonstrates the supply effect of broad upzoning; and the United States, Denmark and Belgium illustrate how mortgage design changes the timing of stress. Four probability-weighted scenarios cover gradual repair, renewed inflationary scarcity, a disorderly correction and a supply-productivity breakthrough. The paper recommends a federal-provincial build-through-cycle framework, infrastructure-linked approvals, public land leasing, countercyclical construction finance, tenure-neutral support, dynamic borrower safeguards, climate-risk pricing and a housing-capacity rule for population planning. The objective is not to guarantee prices, but to preserve real housing value while restoring access and financial resilience.

title: REBUILDING CANADIAN HEALTHCARE After the Pandemic and the Population Shock
affiliations: Szymon Zephan Capital (SZC Group)

detail.title: REBUILDING CANADIAN HEALTHCARE After the Pandemic and the Population Shock

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I am a Managing Partner at SZC Group
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: SZC Group

detail.abstract: A concrete federal-provincial agenda for capacity, access and accountability-with Ontario and Quebec as principal case studies Central judgment. COVID-19 exposed the fragility of a system already operating near full capacity. Rapid population growth in 2022-2024 then widened the gap between demand and deployable supply. Lower planned inflows now reduce the rate at which that gap grows, but they do not close it. Canada requires a population-responsive, access-conditioned and productivity-focused health compact-not another unconditional transfer.

title: Guided Hallucination: Disciplined Projection and the Two Regimes of Truth in AI Career Intelligence

detail.title: Guided Hallucination: Disciplined Projection and the Two Regimes of Truth in AI Career Intelligence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There is no conflict of interest and I have funded my own research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: We operate with the highest ethics and there are no participants or patients where approval is needed for publication of this work.
declarations.funderStatement: We have no funding and our early revenue.

detail.abstract: The dominant safety standard for artificial intelligence in high-stakes applications is the elimination of hallucination. That standard is correct wherever a verifiable fact exists. It is incomplete wherever the task is to describe a future that has not yet produced a fact to verify. Career intelligence for displaced workers occupies both conditions at once. A worker needs the exact wage of a job that exists today, and a credible read on the job that does not exist yet but is forming at the edge of a structural trend. The first demand requires zero tolerance for invention. The second cannot be satisfied without it. This paper argues that the contradiction is resolved not by choosing between the two but by separating them into distinct operating regimes, governed by opposite rules and joined by a single non-negotiable law: the reader must always know which regime they are reading. We describe the implementation of this architecture in a production career intelligence platform, present a worked example from a live report, and specify the conditions under which the approach should be judged to have failed.

title: Metabolic Constraints on Economic Rationality NAD + Decline, Prefrontal Bioenergetics, and the Biological Micro-Foundations of Generational Capital Flow
affiliations: Delphi Wealth Partners

detail.title: Metabolic Constraints on Economic Rationality NAD + Decline, Prefrontal Bioenergetics, and the Biological Micro-Foundations of Generational Capital Flow

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares the following interest, which may be considered a potential competing interest: the author is the founder of Delphi Wealth Partners, a registered investment advisory practice, and the author of a companion working paper (Tice 2026a) advancing a related market-level thesis. This interest is disclosed in full. The hypothesis advanced here is constructed to be falsifiable on independent biological grounds, and its predictions stand or fall on decision-quality and biomarker evidence regardless of any implication for the author's practice. The author declares no other financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This is a theoretical working paper. It reports no new studies involving human participants or animals, and no primary data were collected or analysed. Ethics approval was therefore not required for the present work. The empirical studies proposed in Section VI (Falsifiable Predictions) would, if undertaken, require appropriate institutional ethics review and informed consent; no such approval has been sought or obtained for this paper, and none of those studies has been conducted.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The author received no financial support for the research, authorship, or publication of this article.

detail.abstract: This short-form paper isolates a single mechanism from a larger research program and states it as plainly as possible: economic rationality is a metabolically constrained capacity, and its age-related decline is a thermodynamic phenomenon before it is a psychological one. I propose a seven-link causal chain connecting the age-related fall in nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD +) to a measurable decline in the deliberative (System 2) reasoning on which sound financial decision-making depends: NAD + → ATP → Na + /K +-ATPase → synaptic efficiency → prefrontal cortical (PFC) capacity → System 2 engagement → economic rationality. Each link is an independently characterized dependency drawn from the bioenergetics and cognitive-aging literatures. I then connect this individual-level mechanism to aggregate market behavior: when the same constraint operates across an aging cohort and household decisions are strategic complements rather than independent draws, the result is the demographic capital-flow pattern formalized in the companion paper. The account is deliberately falsifiable-its central prediction is that pairing NAD-precursor supplementation with financial-decision-quality instruments will improve delay discounting and risk assessment in older adults-and its weakest joints are stated openly rather than concealed.

title: Who Wants to Break Up Big Firms? Harm, Fairness, and the Demand for Antitrust
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) and

detail.title: Who Wants to Break Up Big Firms? Harm, Fairness, and the Demand for Antitrust
detail.abstract: The rise of superstar firms has made dominant companies central to modern economic life, and antitrust enforcement is one of the main policy tools for regulating their market power. Public opinion can shape the political and regulatory environment in which antitrust enforcement takes place, yet there is little direct evidence on what drives these preferences. We conduct a pre-registered information-provision experiment with 4,000 American households. Respondents were told about one of five real antitrust cases and randomly assigned to information treatments designed to study four potential drivers of support for antitrust enforcement: perceived market share, perceived consumer harm, perceived unfair competition, and perceived negative image. All four treatments moved the beliefs they were designed to affect, but their effects on demand for antitrust differed sharply. Information about consumer harm had the most systematic effects: it increased plaintiff support and support for break-up and conduct remedies, with effects remaining visible one month later, and also spilled over to broader support for antitrust policies. By contrast, and contrary to expert forecasts, information about market share had no meaningful effect on demand for antitrust enforcement. The findings suggest that the public thinks like economists in one key respect: they do not care about market share per se, but respond instead to consumer harm. One factor outside the core economic framework, perceived unfair competition, also matters, though its effects are more limited in scope. We discuss implications for policymakers and regulators.

title: Distributed Auditing of Cognitive Balance in History Textbooks: Application of the CAP Protocol within a Pre-Service Teacher Network

detail.title: Distributed Auditing of Cognitive Balance in History Textbooks: Application of the CAP Protocol within a Pre-Service Teacher Network
detail.abstract: Background: Despite theorists like Sam Wineburg emphasizing the development of historical thinking, history textbooks in centralized educational systems continue to be dominated by rote-learning approaches, leaving the systematic evaluation of their cognitive balance—particularly at the upper secondary level—largely neglected. • Objective: This study aims to analyze the cognitive balance of upper secondary history textbooks (History 1, 2, 3, and Contemporary History of Iran) and evaluate the efficacy of the Comparative Adjudication Protocol (CAP) within a network of human auditors. • Methodology: Engaging 43 pre-service teachers divided into 15 independent research teams, this study analyzed the content of 4 textbooks comprising 61 independent lessons using the William Romey technique and the CAP protocol. The process was executed across four distinct phases: capacity building, independent AI-assisted auditing, blind peer auditing, and discrepancy adjudication. • Findings: The overall text involvement index was exceptionally low (0.019), far below the active learning threshold of 0.4, with 96.7% of the lessons falling into the passive "banking education" category. The image involvement index was absolute zero (0), and while the question involvement index was 1.29 (with an unbalanced distribution ranging from ∞ to 0.06), it revealed a severe structural gap between passive textual content and active analytical expectations. The CAP protocol demonstrated high reliability, achieving an 86.4% final inter-rater agreement and yielding a 12.5% increase in initial consensus. The dominant discrepancy pattern (A vs. B at 48.3%) indicated that distinguishing "objective historical facts" from "author interpretation" remains the primary analytical challenge for human coders in historical texts. Conclusion: Despite their narrative essence, high school history textbooks exhibit a highly passive cognitive structure lacking a coherent strategy to foster active student engagement. Implementing the CAP protocol within the R2A-TACI-PACT conceptual framework underscores the vital necessity of a "Human-in-the-Loop" (HITL) approach in historical content analysis. Curriculum revision and empowering pre-service teachers with algorithmic auditing literacy are highly recommended.

title: Industrial Policy as Compensation for Economic Decline: Evidence from Post-War Britain

detail.title: Industrial Policy as Compensation for Economic Decline: Evidence from Post-War Britain
detail.abstract: Policies to attract new industries to declining regions are often promoted as remedies for labor-market disruptions from globalization, technology, and energy transitions. This paper argues that these policies do more than redistribute income; place-based industrial policy reshapes the electorate by increasing the size of social groups tied to rising industries. I demonstrate this in the context of the UK in the 1960s, which confronted trade-induced declines in traditional industries such as textiles, coal mining, and shipbuilding. Using newly digitized archival data across two research designs, I study the Local Employment Acts, which steered new industries to areas with high unemployment. The policy reduced unemployment in the medium term and boosted support for Labour-despite originating with the Conservatives. Probing mechanisms, industrial policy shifted the electorate toward higher-skilled manual workers, who tended to back Labour, through selective migration and occupational upgrading. Leaders therefore face incentives to adopt industrial policy when it reweights the electorate toward their likely supporters.

title: Forecasting Greek Deposit Flows
affiliations: Athens University of Economics and Business - Department of Business Administration

detail.title: Forecasting Greek Deposit Flows

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract: We study the predictability of Greek private-sector bank deposit flows at horizons of one, three, six and twelve months, with the one-year horizon as the focal case for liquidity and funding planning. Using monthly ECB Balance Sheet Items data on flow-adjusted deposit transactions of households and non-financial corporations over 2003-02-01 to 2026-05-01 (280 observations), together with a broad set of macro-financial and uncertainty predictors, we run a fully real-time, expanding-window forecasting horse-race across eighteen competing specifications, naive benchmarks, univariate timeseries models, multivariate and machine-learning models, and forecast combinations. Forecasts are strictly out-of-sample over 2014-01-01-2026-05-01 (149 monthly origins) and are ranked by RMSE, MAE, MASE, out-of-sample R-squared and directional accuracy, with Diebold-Mariano tests and the Model Confidence Set used for formal inference. Three results stand out. First, forecast combinations deliver the lowest RMSE and the largest out-of-sample R-squared for total (33.7%) and household flows, whereas for corporate flows the random walk is the model to beat. Second, predictability is strongly heterogeneous across sectors: corporate deposit flows are the most persistent and forecastable, household flows the least. Third, and importantly, none of the models significantly outperforms the random-walk benchmark at the twelve-month horizon in a Diebold-Mariano sense, although at shorter horizons of one to six months the best models do beat it significantly, underscoring that annual-ahead deposit-flow forecasting is intrinsically hard and that the large crisis-driven outflows of 2012 and 2015 were essentially unforecastable one year in advance. We provide a transparent, reproducible pipeline and a forward outlook for the next twelve months. The findings are directly relevant for liquidity monitoring, deposit-based funding planning and macroprudential surveillance.

title: When Stronger Private Enforcement of Securities Law Lowers Stock Prices: Evidence from China's Financial Courts
affiliations: The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Law

detail.title: When Stronger Private Enforcement of Securities Law Lowers Stock Prices: Evidence from China's Financial Courts
detail.abstract: How does stronger private enforcement of securities law affect stock prices? Using China's expansion of financial-court jurisdiction as a quasi-natural experiment, this paper documents a negative stock-price response. The paper's main evidence comes from cumulative-abnormalreturn (CAR) event studies around the enforcement-expansion announcements: the all-treated portfolio loses approximately 3.2 percent over a ten-trading-day ([0, +9]) window, and the estimate is nearly identical for firms with no prior firm-level violation finding. A complementary first-stage analysis finds that financial-court jurisdiction is associated with roughly two-and-a-half times the hazard of a private securities lawsuit after a disclosure-related sanction. Within the no-prior-finding subsample, the announcement decline is significantly larger for firms with higher ex ante securities-fraud risk, linking the price response specifically to securities-fraud enforcement rather than to other functions of financial courts. The pattern is consistent with a one-time capitalization of enforcement exposure-the repricing of liability for misconduct predating the reform.

title: Selecting Active Equity Mutual Funds: A Multi-Signal Approach
affiliations: and

detail.title: Selecting Active Equity Mutual Funds: A Multi-Signal Approach
detail.abstract: We design a quantitative yet tractable model for selecting actively managed equity mutual funds. The proposed model is grounded in academic literature and incorporates information from 30 predictor variables. Using an out-of-sample backtest covering the period from 2010 to 2025, we show that the framework identifies funds which, net-of-fees, outperform the average actively managed fund by 1.68% to 2.64% per annum, a passive investment benchmark by 0.96% to 2.16% per annum, while approximately matching the performance of more complex machine learning models. Our findings suggest that investors improve fund selection outcomes using a scientifically grounded and operationally implementable model.

title: Multimodal Integration of Ambulatory ECG and Clinical Features for Sudden Cardiac Death and Pump Failure Death Prediction
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Multimodal Integration of Ambulatory ECG and Clinical Features for Sudden Cardiac Death and Pump Failure Death Prediction
detail.abstract: Ambulatory electrocardiograms (ECG) provides continuous monitoring of the heart's electrical activity. However, many existing machine learning and artificial intelligence models for analyzing ambulatory ECG traces are often unimodal and do not incorporate patient clinical context. In this study, we propose a multimodal framework integrating ambulatory ECG-derived representations with clinical text embeddings to predict two cardiac outcomes: sudden cardiac death and pump failure death. Ambulatory ECG traces are preprocessed, segmented, and encoded via a multiple instance learning and temporal convolutional neural network framework. In parallel, patient clinical features are parsed into structured prompts, which are passed through a large language model to generate clinical reasoning; this reasoning passes through a biomedical language encoder to generate a text embedding. With the ECG and text embeddings, we systematically evaluate multiple fusion strategies, including concatenation- and gating-based approaches, to integrate these two data modalities. Our results demonstrate that multimodal models consistently outperform unimodal baselines, with adaptive fusion mechanisms providing the greatest improvements in predictive performance. Decision curve analysis highlights the potential clinical utility of the proposed framework for risk stratification. Finally, we visualize model attention across modalities, including ECG attention patterns, segment-level saliency, heart rate variability features, and clinical reasoning, to contextualize patient-specific predictions.

title: Comparative Analysis of Traditional and Deep Learning-Based Speckle Noise Reduction Techniques in Ultrasound Imaging

detail.title: Comparative Analysis of Traditional and Deep Learning-Based Speckle Noise Reduction Techniques in Ultrasound Imaging

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest. This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The author has no personal or financial relationships with any organizations that could have influenced this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, animals, or patient data. All data used in this research were obtained from publicly available datasets (BUSI - Breast Ultrasound Images Dataset). Therefore, no ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Ultrasound imaging is one of the most widely utilized diagnostic modalities due to its safety, costeffectiveness, portability, and ability to provide real-time visualization of soft tissues. However, the presence of speckle noise remains a major limitation, as it reduces image quality, obscures fine anatomical details, and may negatively influence clinical interpretation and computer-aided diagnosis. Over the years, numerous conventional despeckling techniques have been developed to reduce speckle noise while maintaining important structural information. These approaches include adaptive filtering methods, wavelet-based techniques, fuzzy logic approaches, and non-local similarity-based methods. Although effective in certain applications, traditional methods often encounter challenges in achieving an optimal balance between noise suppression and preservation of tissue boundaries and diagnostic features. Recent advances in deep learning have introduced new opportunities for ultrasound image despeckling by enabling models to learn complex noise characteristics directly from large-scale ultrasound datasets. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs), U-Net-based architectures, generative adversarial networks (GANs), residual learning frameworks, and CNN-transformer hybrid models have demonstrated enhanced capability in suppressing speckle noise while preserving anatomical structures and improving image reconstruction quality. This review provides a comparative analysis of traditional and deep learning-based despeckling approaches based on key performance indicators, including noise reduction capability, edge preservation, structural similarity, peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), mean squared error (MSE), clinical applicability, and computational requirements. Despite significant progress, several challenges remain before deep learning-based despeckling methods can be widely adopted in clinical environments. These challenges include the limited availability of highquality annotated ultrasound datasets, variations in imaging conditions affecting model generalization, high computational demands, and difficulties associated with real-time deployment. Addressing these limitations through improved datasets, efficient architectures, and clinically validated frameworks is essential for developing reliable and practical ultrasound despeckling solutions.

title: Litigation Penalties and Bank Lending: Evidence from U.S. Bank Holding Companies
affiliations: , University of Memphis and Texas A&M International University

detail.title: Litigation Penalties and Bank Lending: Evidence from U.S. Bank Holding Companies
detail.abstract: We examine how a bank's own litigation exposure shapes its subsequent lending. Consolidated FR Y-9C filings for U.S. bank holding companies, matched to litigation penalties from 2007 through 2024, show a qualifying penalty followed by slower loan growth in the quarter ahead. The pullback is uneven across offenses. Government and competition matters cut lending most, while employment-related sanctions leave it untouched. Loan-loss provisioning eases over the same window even as nonperforming loans hold steady, a configuration that fits anticipatory caution rather than deterioration in the existing book. The lending result survives staggered difference-indifferences estimators built for heterogeneous treatment timing, and it does not rest on the handful of money-center banks that account for most penalties. The evidence points to a precautionary adjustment in credit supply, one that works quarter to quarter rather than a lasting repricing of risk.

title: The Paradox of Wealth: Why Money Flows to Where It's Least Valuable

detail.title: The Paradox of Wealth: Why Money Flows to Where It's Least Valuable
detail.abstract: The declining marginal welfare value of income is a foundational result in welfare economics. This paper establishes a distinct implication of that result: an increasing monetary reward schedule, combined with diminishing marginal welfare value, produces an income distribution whose ordering is the inverse of the distribution of marginal welfare value. Individuals receiving larger monetary rewards therefore occupy the positions at which an additional dollar generates smaller direct welfare gains. Under logarithmic utility, the relationship is exactly reciprocal, so proportional increases in income produce equal proportional decreases in marginal welfare value. Under any strictly increasing and strictly concave utility function, exact reciprocity need not hold, but the inverse ordering remains. This result is termed the Paradox of Wealth. The analysis distinguishes productive value, incentive value, and marginal welfare value and derives the direct welfare hurdle that a payment to a lower-marginal-welfare-value recipient must overcome through productive, behavioral, institutional, or dynamic benefits. The result applies to income distributions generated by increasing monetary reward schedules in settings involving incentive design, compensation, the allocation of new income, investment, public revenue and expenditure, inequality, and economic growth.

title: Money or Credit, Operationalised: A Comment on Digital Money, the Eighth Future of Banking report

detail.title: Money or Credit, Operationalised: A Comment on Digital Money, the Eighth Future of Banking report

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This is pure independent research.
declarations.funderStatement: Personal research with no outside funding.

detail.abstract: Is a digital euro-claim that promises to be worth one euro a new kind of money, or a new kind of bank? And does the answer depend on who issues it? Digital Money, the eighth Future of Banking report, gives the right answer to the first question and most of the right answer to the second. It treats digital money as a question of monetary architecture rather than technology, judges instruments by the institutions that stand behind them, likens stablecoins to money-market funds, and concludes that tokenised bank deposits are the better-positioned form of private digital money. This comment agrees, and is offered in that spirit. It adds five refinements from two vantage points the report, working globally and at the level of principle, had less room to develop: the operational detail of the European Union’s Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA), and the economic history of offshore money. First, the report’s verdict that “MiCA provides no central-bank backstop” is true of only half the regime, because the issuer is the fork. Second, the three-country comparison gains from an organising principle, a trilemma between par stability, private credit and the absence of a backstop. Third, “functional equivalence” is necessary but not sufficient, because the legal category still governs which risks supervisors are told to watch. Fourth, the report passes over a concrete consumer-protection gap that its own conclusion implies. Fifth, “no backstop” is, at systemic scale, an illusion, and saying so sharpens the report’s strongest point into a clean policy choice. Two of the five are external to the report: the bank/non-bank split inside MiCA’s own e-money-token category, and a deposit-guarantee gap that reaches even bank-issued tokens. The other three reformulate the report’s own logic rather than contest it.

title: Circulation or Category? A Null Result on the Boundary of the Lender of Last Resort

detail.title: Circulation or Category? A Null Result on the Boundary of the Lender of Last Resort

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Independent research - no interest.
declarations.funderStatement: Personal research and personally funded.

detail.abstract: What sets the boundary of the safety net? In a crisis a central bank rescues some private near-monies and lets others fail, and a tempting answer to which is that rescue tracks an entity’s position in the payment, settlement and collateral plumbing (its “circulation-centrality”) rather than its size or its legal category. This paper builds that hypothesis into a falsifiable test and reports that it fails. On a panel of thirty rescue decisions from 1970 to 2023, a blind-coded index of circulation-centrality at first appears to separate the rescued from the abandoned. The appearance does not survive scrutiny. Blind coding removes a thirteen-point hindsight inflation in the author’s own scoring; dropping two index components that quietly restate the rescue trigger removes the construct’s circular content; and correcting two contested keystone cases, Lehman Brothers (whom the Federal Reserve could have saved, per Ball 2018) and Washington Mutual (whose depositors were in fact protected), removes the rest. Conditioning on legal-political capacity rather than deleting the inconvenient cases, the circulation signal falls to a partial correlation of 0.13 (p = 0.53) and is out-predicted by a plain systemic-importance indicator. When an independent coder, blind to the hypothesis, reconstructs the capacity and mandate covariates, the signal does not appear at all (partial r = −0.26, not significant). The boundary of last-resort lending is governed by size and political-legal capacity, the familiar too-big-to-fail account, not by a distinct circulation construct. We offer the test as a reusable template and the false positive as a cautionary anatomy: a strong-looking result manufactured by circular proxies, conditioning-by-deletion, and two miscoded historical cases.

title: Distributed Auditing of Cognitive Balance in History Textbooks: Application of the CAP Protocol within a Pre-Service Teacher Network

detail.title: Distributed Auditing of Cognitive Balance in History Textbooks: Application of the CAP Protocol within a Pre-Service Teacher Network
detail.abstract: Background: Despite theorists like Sam Wineburg emphasizing the development of historical thinking, history textbooks in centralized educational systems continue to be dominated by rote-learning approaches, leaving the systematic evaluation of their cognitive balance—particularly at the upper secondary level—largely neglected. • Objective: This study aims to analyze the cognitive balance of upper secondary history textbooks (History 1, 2, 3, and Contemporary History of Iran) and evaluate the efficacy of the Comparative Adjudication Protocol (CAP) within a network of human auditors. • Methodology: Engaging 43 pre-service teachers divided into 15 independent research teams, this study analyzed the content of 4 textbooks comprising 61 independent lessons using the William Romey technique and the CAP protocol. The process was executed across four distinct phases: capacity building, independent AI-assisted auditing, blind peer auditing, and discrepancy adjudication. • Findings: The overall text involvement index was exceptionally low (0.019), far below the active learning threshold of 0.4, with 96.7% of the lessons falling into the passive "banking education" category. The image involvement index was absolute zero (0), and while the question involvement index was 1.29 (with an unbalanced distribution ranging from ∞ to 0.06), it revealed a severe structural gap between passive textual content and active analytical expectations. The CAP protocol demonstrated high reliability, achieving an 86.4% final inter-rater agreement and yielding a 12.5% increase in initial consensus. The dominant discrepancy pattern (A vs. B at 48.3%) indicated that distinguishing "objective historical facts" from "author interpretation" remains the primary analytical challenge for human coders in historical texts. Conclusion: Despite their narrative essence, high school history textbooks exhibit a highly passive cognitive structure lacking a coherent strategy to foster active student engagement. Implementing the CAP protocol within the R2A-TACI-PACT conceptual framework underscores the vital necessity of a "Human-in-the-Loop" (HITL) approach in historical content analysis. Curriculum revision and empowering pre-service teachers with algorithmic auditing literacy are highly recommended.

title: The Social Value of a Smile: Hard and Soft Information in Trust Games
affiliations: Shandong University - Center for Economic Research, Shandong University - School of Economics and Shandong University - Center for Economic Research

detail.title: The Social Value of a Smile: Hard and Soft Information in Trust Games
detail.abstract: On a daily basis, individuals encounter different types of information signals about other individuals' trustworthiness, and decide which signals are most worthy. Using controlled laboratory experiments, we investigate how hard information on an individual's prior track record versus visual information in the form of a personal photograph shape trust in a laboratory trust game. Trustors in three baseline treatments observe one of three possible signals about their randomly assigned trustee: the trustee's firstround action, a non-smiling photo of their trustee, or a smiling photo of their trustee. Two additional treatments use multiple price lists to elicit trustors' willingness to pay for the trustee's first-round track record relative to the two types of photos. Smiling photos are the only information signal that significantly increases trust and total surplus on average. Information about trustees' first-round track record has no average effect, but masks an asymmetry that favorable records raise trust to the same level as smiling photos, while unfavorable records reduce trust below the level induced by non-smiling photos. The multiple price list and baseline treatments together show that trustors are willing to pay to observe their trustee's first-round track record rather than their photo, while smiling photos in fact generate the highest trust levels. This result highlights a disparity between the type of information individuals prefer, and the type of information they respond positively to, with industrial policy consequences for online platforms and other businesses.

title: Monitoring One-Sided Hypotheses at the Boundary of the Parameter Space: Functional Limit Theory for Expanding-Sample Inference under Inequality Restrictions

detail.title: Monitoring One-Sided Hypotheses at the Boundary of the Parameter Space: Functional Limit Theory for Expanding-Sample Inference under Inequality Restrictions
detail.abstract: Applied work increasingly re-tests a one-sided hypothesis as data accumulate: an inequality restriction maintained by economic theory-no technological regress in a benchmarked frontier, a non-negative variance component, a sign-restricted policy trend-is checked at each vintage of an expanding sample, with the null value sitting on the boundary of the parameter space. Each vintage's test has the nonstandard χ2 limit of Chernoff (1954) and Self and Liang (1987); the monitoring literature descending from Chu et al. (1996) supplies sequential size control, but only for two-sided, interior-parameter problems. This paper joins the two. For expanding-sample constrained M-estimation with the monitored parameter on the boundary, we prove a uniform-in-vintage quadratic expansion and derive the functional limit of the one-sided likelihood-ratio path: Brownian motion in information time, max{0, B(J(r))/ J(r)} 2 , where J(r) is the profiled Fisher information at sample fraction r. For the empirically leading case of a monitored linear trend, J(r) ∝ r 3-not the r of location-parameter monitoring-and the limit is a stationary Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process in 3 log r, yielding exact asymptotic monitoring boundaries, closed-form local-power tilts under Pitman drift c T-3/2 , and detection-delay rates of order b/c. The monitoring constants under the limit law form a design-free two-parameter family in the number of vintages and the initial sample fraction, which we tabulate; the conventional Bonferroni correction is conservative at every design, and its deficiency grows with monitoring intensity. The theory is robust in ways that matter for panel applications: time-invariant unit heterogeneity is annihilated algebraically by the demeaned trend, and arbitrary within-unit dependence and misspecification are handled by a fixed-T cluster-calibrated boundary with proven size control. An end-to-end demonstration on a simulated benchmarking panel exhibits a drift that the exact boundary detects and the Bonferroni scheme misses.

title: Assessing the Feasibility of Adapting Singapore's Housing Model to Honolulu
affiliations: Singapore Management University - School of Economics

detail.title: Assessing the Feasibility of Adapting Singapore's Housing Model to Honolulu
detail.abstract: In response to Hawaii's affordable housing crisis, this paper examines the applicability of Singapore's housing model to Honolulu, focusing on leasehold tenure, revenue-neutral financing, and buyer eligibility regulations. Honolulu's median price-to-income ratio of 10.5 for single-family homes contrasts with about 4.3–4.9 for Singapore's HDB resale flats. Key barriers in Hawaii include historical resistance to leasehold tenure, fragmented housing agencies, limited fiscal capacity, and anticipated opposition to buyer restrictions. However, legislation enacted in 2022–2023 empowering three housing agencies to develop and sell 99-year leasehold housing signals potential for incremental adaptation. While full replication of Singapore's model is unlikely, selective elements may inform policy innovation in Hawaii's housing strategy — and Hawaii's experience offers lessons for other jurisdictions seeking to draw on Singapore's housing framework.

reference: University of Cambridge Faculty of Law Research Paper No. 16/2026
title: Exploring Computational Approaches to Law: The Evolution of Judicial Language in the Anglo-Welsh Poor Law, 1691-1834
affiliations: University of Cambridge - Centre for Business Research (CBR) and University of Cambridge - Cambridge Judge Business School

detail.title: Exploring Computational Approaches to Law: The Evolution of Judicial Language in the Anglo-Welsh Poor Law, 1691-1834

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Cambridge Faculty of Law Research Paper No. 16/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Cambridge Faculty of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The use of natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning (ML) to analyse the structure of legal texts is a fast-growing field. While much attention has been devoted to the use of these techniques to predict case outcomes, they have the potential to contribute more broadly to research into the nature of legal reasoning and its relationship to social and economic change. In this paper, we use recently developed NLP and ML methods to test the claim that judicial language is systematically shaped by economic shocks deriving from the business cycle and by long-run trends in the economy associated with technological change and industrial transition. Focusing on cases decided under the Anglo-Welsh poor law between the 1690s and 1830s, we show that the terminology used to describe the right to poor relief shifted over time according to economic conditions. We explore the implications of our results for the poor law, the theory of legal evolution, and socio-legal research methods.

title: Freedom in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Why Relief Is Not the Same as Freedom
affiliations: Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi Christian University Inc.

detail.title: Freedom in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Why Relief Is Not the Same as Freedom

keywords: Freedom in the Age Of AI

detail.abstract:
This article analyzes freedom in the age of artificial intelligence in connection with the diagnosis of Existential Alignment developed in the preceding article. At its center is not the question of whether artificial intelligence directly replaces human decisions. Rather, it works out how self-determination changes when spaces of choice are al ready ordered before the decision is made. Freedom then appears no longer merely as the possibility of choosing, but as the ability still to recognize and examine the con ditions of one’s own choice.
The text connects this question with empirical findings on choice overload, valence formation, automation bias, default effects, recommendation systems, and self-deter mination. It shows that more options do not necessarily lead to more freedom. At the same time, it becomes visible how technical relief can replace one’s own examination and how preordered plausibilities become effective precisely when they appear as help. The new unfreedom does not primarily operate as coercion, but as facilitated self direction.
The article shows why self-determination is more than the possibility of choosing and why an AI-supported lifeworld can both facilitate and weaken freedom. The concluding question of a form of existence that does not fully dissolve into prepared plausibilities is reserved for the following contribution on Existential Non-Absorption.

title: QT Is Not Simply Reverse QE: Inference Using HARS-Z

detail.title: QT Is Not Simply Reverse QE: Inference Using HARS-Z
detail.abstract: I develop HARS-Z by extending HARS, the sampler of Kim and Zha (2026), to include zero restrictions alongside shock heteroskedasticity, sign restrictions, and narrative restrictions. Using HARS-Z, I estimate how the transmission of balance-sheet policy to real GDP and the price level depends on the liability that finances it. On monthly U.S. data I identify two balance-sheet shocks, one financed by reserves and one by overnight reverse repurchases (ON RRP). The estimated transmission differs across the two financing channels. A reserve-financed expansion raises GDP and the GDP deflator, and an ON RRP-financed contraction lowers them, but the magnitudes of the responses are asymmetric, especially for the deflator. Even under the same financing liability, local projections show no evidence that quantitative tightening (QT) is the reverse of quantitative easing (QE).

title: Technological Innovation and Institutional Quality: Drivers of Green Economic Growth in Selected Arab Countries (2010-2023)
affiliations: Future University in Egypt FUE

detail.title: Technological Innovation and Institutional Quality: Drivers of Green Economic Growth in Selected Arab Countries (2010-2023)
detail.abstract: Amid mounting environmental constraints and the push for economic diversification away from hydrocarbon dependence, green growth has emerged as a priority strategy. The research aims to analyze the impact of innovation and institutional quality on green economic growth in selected Arab countries (Egypt, Jordan, Morocco, Tunisia, and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) over the period from 2010 to 2023. The empirical analysis draws on panel data and applies a fixed-effects regression framework to account for country-specific heterogeneity and time-invariant unobserved factors, the key variables include the Green Growth Index, the Innovation Index, patent applications, the rule of law, and government efficiency. The empirical results showed that innovation has a limited impact on green growth, while patents contribute significantly to improving green economic performance. The rule of law also showed a strong positive effect, underscoring the importance of institutional quality. These findings reflect the need to promote technological innovation and strengthen institutional frameworks that support sustainable development in the Arab region, in line with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

title: From Numbers to Words: Breaking Down Institutional Beliefs
affiliations: Bocconi University and London Business School

detail.title: From Numbers to Words: Breaking Down Institutional Beliefs
detail.abstract: Using Capital Market Assumptions (CMA) reports, in which managers publish long-horizon forecasts and explain how they construct them, we show how they form beliefs about returns, volatilities, and correlations. They decompose return expectations into broad building blocks across asset classes, but assign different values to them. For U.S. equity, valuation change is the largest net source of disagreement. Growth expectations, however, partly offset valuation-change expectations because the two are strongly negatively correlated, so return expectations understate disagreement in the underlying views. In most non-U.S. equity markets, growth is the main source of disagreement. This matters for portfolios: equity allocations load about twice as strongly on growth expectations as on valuation-change expectations. Three mechanisms shape belief formation: managers anchor to peer consensus, use different modeling assumptions, and process information through narratives that differ in complexity and topic attention. Modeling assumptions such as mean reversion and historical calibration predict systematic forecast differences. Narrative complexity and topic attention predict responses to news: managers with more complex or valuation-focused narratives respond less to positive earnings news, whereas attention to dividend yield or downturn risks is associated with stronger responses. Comparisons with N-CSR shareholder letters show that CMA narratives reflect persistent institution-specific investment views. Volatility and correlation beliefs, by contrast, remain backward-looking.

title: Social Norms and Coordination in a Threshold Public Good Game with Increasing Group Size

detail.title: Social Norms and Coordination in a Threshold Public Good Game with Increasing Group Size
detail.abstract: Social norms can help coordinate within groups. When the group size increases with uncertainty, existing coordination may be unstable. This project employs a laboratory experiment to investigate the persistence of social norms and their influence on coordination behaviors in a threshold public good game with increasing group size. Participants will first choose one of two norms. They will then be randomly assigned a role and put into a group of four. A group starts with one member, and a new member joins with a 25% chance until the group size reaches 4. Members A and B agree on the same norm in treatment groups, while A and B differ in norm choices in control groups. C and D's norm choices are unknown in both cases. In each round, current members participate in a public goods game with a threshold of one investment, while observers remain inactive. There are four main findings of this experiment. First, there's no significant difference in the provision rates of public goods between the treatment groups and the control groups. Second, the persistence rates of both norms start higher in treatment groups but decline more rapidly when group size increases than those of the control groups. Third, the overinvestment rate increases with group size, and it is higher when conditional on no investment in the previous round. Last but not least, different response rates among group members are the key reason why a social norm persists for a shorter time. For a social planner who aims to establish a social norm that helps people coordinate as the group expands, it must be a good norm in the sense that people accept it at a similar level, so that it can persist longer.

title: When More History Raises Portfolio Risk: Lookback Windows, Missing Data, and Covariance Nonstationarity in Minimum-Variance Portfolios
affiliations: Goethe University Frankfurt

detail.title: When More History Raises Portfolio Risk: Lookback Windows, Missing Data, and Covariance Nonstationarity in Minimum-Variance Portfolios
detail.abstract: Using more return history can make minimum-variance portfolios riskier. Two channels drive the penalty: longer estimation windows pool across distinct covariance regimes, and they introduce incomplete return histories from IPOs, spin-offs, and mergers. We quantify both on Center for Research in Security Prices daily returns for the 500 largest U.S. stocks (1975-2024), comparing estimators ranging from static shrinkage methods to recursive filters that separate volatility dynamics from correlation estimation. Missing-history handling is the single most consequential design choice: zero-imputing missing returns at a fiveyear lookback nearly doubles realized out-of-sample portfolio volatility, yet at short lookbacks the problem is negligible. Choosing the wrong missing-data rule is several times more costly than choosing the wrong window length. On a fixed universe with complete histories, no single lookback dominates. Separating fast-moving volatility from slower-moving dependence is the only preprocessing that lets longer histories help. At short lookbacks, however, recursive filters and factor-shrinkage baselines deliver indistinguishable performance, so the preprocessing advantage is specific to medium and long windows. The mechanism is covariance nonstationarity: adjacentwindow covariance movement pervasively exceeds the constant-covariance samplingnoise benchmark, with the excess concentrated in high-correlation episodes. Lookback length, missing-history handling, and dependence estimation are joint design choices, not independent defaults.

title: Carbon Pricing, Sovereign Risk, and the Monetary-Fiscal Nexus in the Green Transition
affiliations: and Banque de France

detail.title: Carbon Pricing, Sovereign Risk, and the Monetary-Fiscal Nexus in the Green Transition
detail.abstract: Although the transition to a low-carbon economy is necessary, it acts as a major macroeconomic supply shock that increases energy costs, driving up inflation while depressing economic activity. While fiscal policy can theoretically cushion this negative income shock, its capacity to do so is highly constrained in high-debt countries, where a carbon-policy shock triggers a "double tightening": monetary policy reacts to curb rising inflation, while financial markets simultaneously price in greater sovereign risk. This mechanism is documented empirically for the euro area using high-frequency surprises in the Emissions Trading System to isolate carbon-policy shocks, with quarterly local projections confirming that these shocks are stagflationary and persistently widen the sovereign spreads of high-debt countries relative to low-debt ones. To explain these dynamics, the paper develops and estimates a Two-Agent New Keynesian model with disaggregated energy production, built around an endogenous fiscal limit where the maximum sustainable debt falls alongside output, forcing sovereign spreads to respond directly to the economic cycle. The model reveals that the welfare cost of the transition is strictly debt-contingent: while low-debt countries absorb the shock with minimal financial market pressure, high-debt countries experience severe spread widening that can only be mitigated by how carbon revenues are recycled. Using these revenues to pay down public debt secures a vital "fiscal dividend" that narrows spreads, whereas rebating them to households forgoes this stabilization, demonstrating that adequate fiscal space is a fundamental precondition for reconciling climate ambition with macroeconomic and financial stability.

title: Closed-Form Threshold Bounds for Joint Hedging and Poisson Forfeiture in CARA Optimal Stopping

detail.title: Closed-Form Threshold Bounds for Joint Hedging and Poisson Forfeiture in CARA Optimal Stopping
detail.abstract: We study a perpetual optimal stopping problem with exponential utility in which a nontraded payoff can be partially hedged and the investment opportunity may be lost at an independent Poisson time. At the Poisson event the opportunity lapses and the agent retains financial wealth only. Under risk neutrality such a loss would act as extra discounting; here it instead pulls the value toward the Merton benchmark. In the finite-threshold regimes, partial hedging and forfeiture each lead on their own to an optimal threshold in closed form through the Lambert W function. When both frictions are present, this closed-form structure is lost. The value threshold is the largest smooth-pasting root along an autonomous phase-plane branch, and the associated stopping rule and feedback portfolio are verified for arbitrary effective drift. The threshold lies between two explicit Lambert W bounds, which collapse to equality in the absence of hedging interaction and provide a computable localization of the joint threshold.

title: The Deep-Pockets Premium: Visible Wealth and Negotiated Prices in Football Transfers
affiliations: and Chapman University - The George L. Argyros College of Business and Economics

detail.title: The Deep-Pockets Premium: Visible Wealth and Negotiated Prices in Football Transfers
detail.abstract: Bargaining theory and OTC evidence hold that better-resourced buyers obtain better prices; both assume the buyer's reservation value is private. We show that when the buyer's financial capacity is publicly visible, the pattern inverts: wealthier buyers pay a deep-pockets premium for comparable assets, consistent with sellers conditioning on capacity to pay. In football transfers, where financial capacity is unusually visible, fees rise 7 to 15% within the same buyer and transfer window once its large sale becomes public. A buyer ten times larger pays 100% more for a comparable player, and 45% more for the same player under player, buyer-club, and contemporaneous-quality controls. Overpayment is associated with more playing time conditional on observable quality, consistent with acquisition-price anchoring. A partial-equilibrium mapping corresponds to 8 to 17% of fees, €314-628 million annually, flowing from large buyers primarily to selling clubs. Budget disclosure can increase seller rent extraction in negotiated markets.

title: The Dealer Atom: A Universal Intraday Timescale in Volatility and Its Installation in Cryptocurrency Markets

detail.title: The Dealer Atom: A Universal Intraday Timescale in Volatility and Its Installation in Cryptocurrency Markets
detail.abstract: The autocorrelation of absolute returns in liquid markets contains a fast exponential component with a timescale of one to five trading hours and a modal value of 2.4 hours, a dealer atom, recovered in fourteen traditional measurements across FX, metals, energy and equities and confirmed on sealed holdouts (median 2.1 hours). The component is absent from cryptocurrency markets before the professionalisation of their market-making, and its arrival is datable. Ether acquires the atom in the week of the FTX collapse: six of seven measurements across five venues fall inside a pre-registered window, and the level shift survives volatility orthogonalisation. In January 2024, the month spot-Bitcoin ETFs routed conventional marketmaking into the asset class, ten asset-venue cells on three sealed exchanges acquire it on the identical date, a coincidence carrying p < 1.5 × 10 ⁵ under an independence null. Witness births ⁻ quantise into waves on all three sealed venues; Bitcoin, which professionalised gradually, has no dated birth. Stress-conditional estimation shows the timescale is regime-invariant while its weight moves: a process constant of the hours-scale imbalance-absorbing intermediation layer, with the weight as participation telemetry. All dating follows a written registration protocol with three sealed holdouts, published failures and one retraction.

title: Intergovernmental Grants to School Districts and Educational Outcomes During the COVID-19 Pandemic
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - University of California, San Diego, University of California, San Diego (UCSD) and American Enterprise Institute

detail.title: Intergovernmental Grants to School Districts and Educational Outcomes During the COVID-19 Pandemic

keywords: Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief

detail.abstract: The federal government appropriated $189.5 billion in pandemic aid to school districts through the Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief (ESSER) fund. We evaluate their impact on schools with district poverty shares near 5%, where a threshold-driven increase in funds enables us to implement a difference-in-discontinuities design. Federal funds were passed on to residents through reductions in local revenue collections, including property taxes, and did not result in increased per-pupil expenditures by school districts. We find no evidence that additional funds mitigated the declines in test scores. We provide suggestive evidence that political engagement, especially from parents, increased in districts that qualified for additional funds. This combination of engagement and reduced taxation may explain the greater enrollment and faster reopening we observe in such districts.

title: Building Data Centers: Legal, Financing and Project Development Considerations

detail.title: Building Data Centers: Legal, Financing and Project Development Considerations
detail.abstract:
As artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and digital services continue to expand, data centers are becoming a critical component to the modern digital infrastructure. The growth has a knock on effect on major investment in other areas such as land, power supply, grid access, and construction delivery.

At the same time, data center projects differ from other infrastructure projects mainly due to their high power-consumption, technical and commercial dependence on connectivity and speed, electricity reliability, as well as instant operational performance.

Hence, the development of data centers has its own distinct set of legal and commercial issues. These include among other things siting and permitting constraints, financing and bankability considerations, project delivery method, as well as interfaces between different contracts. While from the outside a data center it looks like a simple building that houses digital equipment, however, from the inside the project, it has all the components of a complex infrastructure project, which to achieve successful delivery requires coherence of the overall contractual and project structure of the players involved.

title: Clinical Trial Data in the European Health Data Space: Secondary Use, Confidentiality and Harmonisation
affiliations: University of Copenhagen - Centre for Advanced Studies in Bioscience Innovation Law (CeBIL),  and The Institute of Law Studies at the Polish Academy of Sciences

detail.title: Clinical Trial Data in the European Health Data Space: Secondary Use, Confidentiality and Harmonisation

declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported, in part, by a Novo Nordisk Foundation Grant for a scientifically independent International Collaborative Bioscience Innovation & Law Programme (Inter-CeBIL programme, grant no. NNF23SA0087056).

detail.abstract: Regulation (EU) 2025/327 places data from clinical trials within the European Health Data Space's (EHDS) regime for the secondary use of electronic health data and thereby reconfigures the legal conditions under which such data may be accessed across the Union. This article argues that, in the clinical trial context, the EHDS serves not just as an additional transparency instrument but further marks a shift from disclosure of regulatory documents to administratively managed access to reusable datasets. That shift requires attention because the EHDS superimposes a new permitting structure, centred on national Health Data Access Bodies, onto an already dense framework consisting of Regulation 1049/2001, European Medicines Agency (EMA) Policies 0043 and 0070, and the Clinical Trials Regulation. Article 52 is the fulcrum of the new regime. It requires electronic health data protected by intellectual property rights, trade secrets or regulatory data protection to be made available for secondary use, subject to safeguards and refusal where serious risk cannot be satisfactorily mitigated. The article shows that this architecture may harmonise access in form while fragmenting it in operation through divergent HDAB practice across Member States. It argues that Article 52 requires a translation exercise between commercially confidential information, trade secrets and regulatory data protection, and proposes coordinated Article 52 guidance and a clinicaltrial-data assessment template aligned with EMA and Clinical Trials Information System (CTIS) practice and Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) confidentiality case law.

title: The First Hour: How Foreign Exchange Absorbs Its Daily Gap

detail.title: The First Hour: How Foreign Exchange Absorbs Its Daily Gap
detail.abstract: At the daily reopen, foreign exchange prices gap: the first hourly bar opens on average 4.8 pips from the prior close, and 74% of these discontinuities exceed one pip. Every other hour averages 0.12 pips. On twelve years of hourly data for six USD pairs (2014-2026), net of per-pair spreads throughout, this paper documents where and how fast that gap is absorbed. Fading reopen gaps of at least one pip and holding for a single hour earns a net profit factor of 2.63 with zero losing years over 2019-2026, and the edge is monotone in gap size, at 3.16 for two pips and 4.69 for five. Holding the identical positions to the daily close roughly halves the profit factor, from 2.63 to 1.18. The identical fade applied to the micro-gaps of hours one through twenty-three loses money in every specification and every year: the mechanism is the daily liquidity auction, not the bar boundary. The pre-2019 half of the sample is marginal at one pip, a regime dependence reported plainly. A Reality Check over the full eighteen-rule search grid rejects at p < 0.0005. The overnight component's reversal is concentrated in the opening auction of a decentralised market.

title: Every Exit Rule Manufactures an Option: An Exit-Invariant Decomposition of Trading-Strategy Expectancy

detail.title: Every Exit Rule Manufactures an Option: An Exit-Invariant Decomposition of Trading-Strategy Expectancy
detail.abstract: Any trading ledger, projected onto the underlying's own post-entry path, yields a nonparametric Greeks decomposition: a quadratic regression of trade profit on the directionadjusted reference move splits expectancy exactly into a theta leg (carry), a gamma leg (convexity paid by realised variance), and a delta leg (directional pass-through). Optional stopping imposes a sharp null. If the underlying is a martingale at the strategy's entry times, then for every exit rule expected profit is zero and the theta leg must exactly offset the gamma leg, a per-trade image of the Black-Scholes relation between time decay and convexity. The gap in that identity is an alpha meter with an exit-invariant null. Applied to a seven-year live book of 11,455 hourly FX fills, the meter reads a structure forbidden without information: long theta and long gamma together, a +2.31-pip violation at 3.5 bootstrap standard errors, stable across horizons, halves, and all six pairs. A random-entry control on the identical machinery manufactures more convexity than the live book and pays fair premium to within a seventh of a pip. A momentum probe reads approximately zero. The statistic certifies possession of entry information, and its size, while revealing nothing of its construction.

title: Assessing Structural Geopolitical Risk *
affiliations: BBVA Research – Ciudad BBVA, BBVA Research – Ciudad BBVA and

detail.title: Assessing Structural Geopolitical Risk *
detail.abstract: This paper introduces a novel measure of Structural Geopolitical Risk (SGR), designed to capture the long-run conditions that shape the likelihood of geopolitical tensions, conflicts, and fragmentation. Complementing existing geopolitical risk measures, the SGR aims to measure the latent structural factors that increase the likelihood of future geopolitical disruptions. Constructed for nearly all countries worldwide over 1960-2025, it combines an internal dimension (ISGR), capturing domestic political, institutional, and military vulnerabilities of each individual country, and crucially, an external dimension (ESGR), reflecting the political environment of different interconnected groups of foreign countries which are weighted by geographical proximity, military relevance, and ideological distance. We show that global SGR has risen steadily since the early 2000s, reaching levels comparable to those of the late Cold War by 2025. Validation exercises indicate that higher SGR is associated with weaker trade and investment, greater financial vulnerability, a higher probability of future conflicts and geopolitical risk events, and a stronger transmission of realized geopolitical shocks to economic activity. Extensive sensitivity analyses confirm the robustness of the indicators dynamics, crosscountry rankings, and economic relationships.

title: Purity as a Parallelisation Contract: Formal Composability Guarantee and Empirical Throughput in Python and Rust Data Pipelines
affiliations: University of Hertfordshire

detail.title: Purity as a Parallelisation Contract: Formal Composability Guarantee and Empirical Throughput in Python and Rust Data Pipelines
detail.abstract: Functional pipelines are routinely claimed to be “safer to parallelise” than their imperative counterparts, but the claim is rarely separated into its provable and its measurable parts. This paper does so explicitly. I formalise a data-processing pipeline as a composition of pure functions over a finite sequence, prove a map-fusion law and a monoid-homomorphism (split-fold) law that together license arbitrary re-partitioning of work without altering the result, and give a semi-formal argument, grounded in Rust's ownership type system, for why a disjoint partition of pure, non-aliasing computations is free of data races by construction. I implement one identical pipeline, filter, normalise, hash, reduce, in Python (functional and imperative styles, with process-based parallelism) and in Rust (sequential iterators and rayon data-parallel iterators), and benchmark both on two hosts of markedly different parallel capacity: a single logical-core sandbox and a 16-core, 22-thread workstation. On the single-core host, neither rayon nor Python's multiprocessing pool improves wall-clock throughput over the sequential baseline, exactly as Amdahl's law predicts when no hardware parallelism is available. With 22 threads available, the same unmodified code achieves genuine speed-ups, up to 7.0× for Rust's rayon pipeline and up to 6.7× for Python's multiprocessing pool, both well below the 22× ideal. Fitting Amdahl's law to the observed speed-ups, using mean timings and their 95% confidence intervals rather than best-of-N figures, shows Rust's implied parallel fraction settling in the 0.87–0.90 range for N ≥ 1,000,000, consistent with a fixed, hardware-bound coordination cost, whereas Python's implied parallel fraction falls from around 0.89 at smaller N to 0.66 at the largest N tested, indicating that its serialisation overhead is not the fixed constant Amdahl's model assumes but grows with data volume. This is a quantitative, falsifiable difference between the two languages' parallel-execution mechanisms, not merely a difference in constant-factor speed, and it is verified empirically through nine bit-for-bit correctness checks across sequential, parallel, and cross-language variants, independently reproduced on both a single pinned core and the 22-thread configuration of the same host.

title: Ontological Acceleration: Infrastructure Pre-Staging, Crisis Exploitation, and the Acceleration of Capitalist Restructuring

detail.title: Ontological Acceleration: Infrastructure Pre-Staging, Crisis Exploitation, and the Acceleration of Capitalist Restructuring
detail.abstract:
How does capitalism survive crises by transforming faster than opposition can organize? This paper proposes the accordion mechanism—a systematic process through which capitalism simultaneously compresses alternatives (squeeze phase) while expanding new infrastructure (expand phase) until genuine choice disappears. The acceleration velocity is exponential: the Industrial Revolution required 100 years to transform peasants into proletarians; the digital transition accomplished similar ontological restructuring in 4 years (2020–2024).

The mechanism operates through two steps: (1) long-term infrastructure pre-staging—building technical, legal, and psychological foundations for future systems decades before mandating adoption—and (2) crisis exploitation—using justified emergencies to convert optional systems into mandatory ones.

Empirically, this paper documents how COVID-19 enabled simultaneous resolution of five pre-existing structural crises that were individually unsolvable through democratic process: cash elimination (squeeze informal economy surveillance), pension system relief (demographic adjustment), real estate intergenerational redistribution (wealth transfer mechanism), labor market restructuring (wage suppression), and unified digital identity deployment (surveillance integration).

The analysis reveals that system transformation accelerated 7-fold during the pandemic period (cash elimination rate 1% annually 2000–2019 vs. 7% annually 2020–2024). A boundary test using Turkey—where infrastructure pre-staging was incomplete and institutional friction remained—confirms that acceleration can be delayed but appears difficult to prevent.

The critical finding: once Central Bank Digital Currencies are deployed and integrated with digital identity systems (projected 2027–2030), reversal becomes technically impossible and politically inconceivable. The window for democratic intervention remains open through 2030, then closes.

The paper concludes that between now and 2030, democratic societies face a binary choice: either permit elite-controlled algorithmic feudalism or consciously redirect technological acceleration toward cooperative alternatives. The outcome depends on what human beings choose to do in the next 5–10 years.

title: A Seat at the Table: Turning AI Macroeconomic Views into Portfolios with a Factor Framework
affiliations: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management and Healthcare of Ontario Pension Plan

detail.title: A Seat at the Table: Turning AI Macroeconomic Views into Portfolios with a Factor Framework
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is everywhere in investing-and yet, when it comes to the core task of deciding how capital is allocated, almost nowhere. This paper offers one concrete answer, worked out end to end and demonstrated with a working system. We keep the process investors already follow-form a view on the economy, then build the portfolio-and make the division of labor explicit. The authors set the analytical frame: AI operates within that frame through a pipeline of agents that gathers and organizes macroeconomic evidence and distills it into probabilistic views on growth and inflation regimes, honest about its own uncertainty. A transparent engine takes the second step, translating any view-machine-generated or human-into candidate portfolios inside hard constraints set by the CIO, the CRO, and the Board. The committee decides throughout: AI gets a seat at the table, not the chair. The engine also runs in an interactive portfolio construction tool developed with AI assistance from author-specified methodology and requirements.

title: Front-Loading the Facts: A Randomized Field Experiment in a DA's Screening Unit
affiliations: Southern Methodist University - Dedman School of Law and Southern Methodist University - Dedman School of Law
