detail.title: Front-Loading the Facts: A Randomized Field Experiment in a DA's Screening Unit

declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded in part by the Chrest Foundation and the Child Poverty Action Lab.

detail.abstract:
Prosecutorial screening decisions determine whether an arrest becomes a criminal prosecution and shape nearly every subsequent stage of the criminal process. Yet there is little rigorous evidence exploring how prosecutors make these decisions, much less how their decision-making practices might be improved. The limited existing scholarship suggests that prosecutors often make their screening (and charging) decisions under conditions of substantial informational uncertainty. Whether reducing that uncertainty affects prosecutorial decision-making remains largely unknown. 

This Article reports the results of a randomized controlled trial conducted in partnership with the Dallas County District Attorney's Office. Researchers and prosecutors jointly designed an intervention that conducted early outreach to complaining witnesses in randomly selected nonintimate-partner assault cases. The study examined two principal outcomes: the time it took prosecutors to screen a police submission ("time-to-decision") and the likelihood that a police submission would be declined for prosecution ("likelihood of declination"). 

The intervention substantially altered both outcomes. Prosecutors’ median time-to-decision declined from 13 days for control cases to 10 days for treatment cases. The intervention also increased the rate of declination from 12.2% to 21.2%. Qualitative data collected from participating prosecutors suggest that early witness outreach reduced prosecutors’ uncertainty regarding witnesses’ availability, cooperation, and credibility, thereby reducing their hesitation about screening (and charging) decisions.

The findings provide rare field-experimental evidence regarding prosecutorial decision-making. More broadly, they suggest that informational uncertainty is not merely a background condition of prosecutorial screening. Rather, informational uncertainty materially influences both the timing and outcome of prosecutors’ screening decisions. By combining experimental and qualitative methods within a functioning prosecutor's office, this study provides evidence regarding both whether an intervention worked and the mechanism through which it appears to have operated.

title: Markup Accounting
affiliations: The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania , University of Western Ontario and Western University

detail.title: Markup Accounting
detail.abstract: We document new facts of markup dispersion across the firm size distribution using a large sample of firms in India, the US, and 10 European countries. The main result is that markup differences between firms of similar size account for over half of the overall dispersion, calling for mechanisms that affect markups beyond market concentration. To study these mechanisms, we develop an analytical oligopolistic competition model of variable markups that accounts for the observed joint distribution of markups and firm size, including the large mass of small firms with high markups and the presence of large firms with small markups. The key ingredient is the introduction of firm-specific demand elasticity shifters that account for differences in markups between firms of similar size. We apply this model to Indian and U.S. firm data and find consistent results throughout. Without demand elasticity shifters, equilibrium markups collapse to those of standard static models of oligopolistic or monopolistic competition, which capture less than half of the observed variation in markups and counterfactually assign most of the variation to differences between firms of different size. In aggregate, the model implies efficiency losses from markup dispersion that are four to ten times larger than those implied by standard models of heterogeneous markups.

title: Regulating the Retail Options Boom: Evidence from India’s 2024–25 Equity Index Derivatives Reforms
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Regulating the Retail Options Boom: Evidence from India’s 2024–25 Equity Index Derivatives Reforms
detail.abstract: Between October 2024 and April 2025 the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) rolled out the most aggressive package of retail derivatives curbs attempted in a major market: a package spanning weekly-expiry rationalization, a threefold in crease in minimum contract size, and tighter margining and position monitoring. We assemble a 48-month panel of exchange-level turnover (April 2022–March 2026, NSE and BSE combined) from SEBI Monthly Bulletin annexure tables and combine it with cohort-level participation data from SEBI’s own studies to provide early causal evidence on the reforms. Using stock options (untargeted by the reforms) as a within-market control, a trend-adjusted difference-in-differences design implies that index-options no tional turnover fell 37–43% below its counterfactual path in the six months following the first wave, while premium turnover fell far less (−13% year on year), consistent with a compositional shift away from deep out-of-the-money weekly contracts. Participation effects were large and fell hardest on the smallest traders, the mechanical incidence of a minimum contract size: unique traders fell 20% year on year, with declines of 25–36 log points concentrated in the smallest turnover cohorts (difference-in-differences esti mate −47 log points, permutation-robust). We find no evidence of substitution into the cash market, which contracted alongside; substitution into products outside our panel cannot be ruled out. Aggregate turnover effects attenuate by FY2026 as activity migrated across exchanges, adapted to larger contracts, and, from January 2026, faced a rule-driven downward recalibration of lot sizes; participation effects persist through the latest available data.

title: Does Listing Language Add Value Beyond Location? Deconfounding Text and Geography in Automated Home Valuation
affiliations: and

detail.title: Does Listing Language Add Value Beyond Location? Deconfounding Text and Geography in Automated Home Valuation
detail.abstract: Automated valuation models increasingly price homes from the prose of a listing, and the added language reliably improves their predictions. Whether it carries information about the property or merely the neighborhood the writing encodes has gone untested, because the two are observationally identical. We separate them not by adjusting for location but by a sequence of designs that hold it fixed ever more strictly. Estimating the effect of listing text on log price by partially linear double machine learning across twelve metropolitan markets, we find that the effect depends on which direction through the sentenceembedding is read as the treatment. The direction that strips the location-predictable channel leaves it near eleven percent per standard deviation. The effect survives holding the building itself fixed, where geography cannot vary, at three and a half percent, and survives at one percent between near-identical units in the same building. Each design removes more of what the estimate could be confounded with. The premium falls as part of the raw association proves to be location and part unit quality, yet it never reaches zero. New York makes this vivid. Its language is the most geographic in the panel, its naive effect a significant negative, and every design that removes location flips it to a significant positive premium there. The surviving premium is modest, but it is identified by holding geography fixed rather than by assuming it away, and the worry that text valuation is mostly relabeled location does not, on this evidence, bear out.

title: Optimal Question Design in Prediction Markets

detail.title: Optimal Question Design in Prediction Markets
detail.abstract: Every prediction market embeds a question: how finely should the outcome be partitioned into tradable contracts? We endogenize this choice in a rational-expectations model where informed capital and liquidity are tied to the state, so each listed contract congests the others. Refinement is not Blackwell-monotone, and a finer question can yield a less informative market. Optimal granularity is interior and inelastic in depth; optimal placement over-samples the tails; Bayesian reading faces a finite resolution ceiling; and refinement transfers surplus from hedgers to insiders. We develop the framework of congested information design and calibrate its design rule to Kalshi's bracket markets.

title: When Does a Regime Layer Earn Its Place? A Sign-Change Criterion with Four Adjudications on a Live Trading Book

detail.title: When Does a Regime Layer Earn Its Place? A Sign-Change Criterion with Four Adjudications on a Live Trading Book
detail.abstract: Trading systems accumulate conditioning layers, regime gates, magnitude loaders, filters on the filter itself, and the question of which earn their place has no standard answer. This paper states one criterion and adjudicates it four times on a single live book of 11,455 automated FX trades over seven years. The criterion follows from mean-variance sizing: a binary regime layer raises attainable per-trade Sharpe over the best continuous sizing on the same information if and only if conditional expectancy changes sign across its states. Gradients without a zero crossing are sizing inputs at most, and under proportional risk-return scaling they are absorbed entirely. On the book, exactly one candidate crosses zero: the performance-regime gate separates +11.0 pips per trade from-6.2 and lifts per-trade Sharpe from 0.059 to 0.188. Three further layers carry real, stable, readable structure and fail as predicted. A meta-reliability state with a two-to-one conditional spread gains +0.0019 at best, its bootstrap interval straddling zero; an intermediation amplitude runs terciles of +4.2, +2.4, +2.3 pips with a shuffle placebo at p = 0.83; and a day-ahead volatility forecast reaches 0.65 out-of-sample correlation against 0.00 for direction. The structure is genuine in every failing case, and the criterion explains why none of it converts.

reference: INDIGENOUS KNOWLEDGE IN INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY: THE UNDRIPS AND THE GOVERNANCE OF GENETIC RESOURCES, Chidi Oguamanam, ed., Cambridge University Press, 2027, Forthcoming
title: Protecting Genetic Resources and Associated Traditional Knowledge in the International Intellectual Property Regime Complex
affiliations: Texas A&M University School of Law

detail.title: Protecting Genetic Resources and Associated Traditional Knowledge in the International Intellectual Property Regime Complex

publicationDetails.detailsText: INDIGENOUS KNOWLEDGE IN INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY: THE UNDRIPS AND THE GOVERNANCE OF GENETIC RESOURCES, Chidi Oguamanam, ed., Cambridge University Press, 2027, Forthcoming

detail.abstract:
This chapter examines the past and ongoing efforts to strengthen global protections for genetic resources and associated traditional knowledge in the international intellectual property regime complex. It begins by identifying these efforts and using them to illustrate the many possibilities for strengthening such protections.

The chapter then explores why an international treaty for protecting genetic resources and associated traditional knowledge was ultimately adopted at the World Intellectual Property Organization. It offers three primary contributing factors: the choice of negotiating forum, the possibility for linkage bargaining, and the timing of the negotiations.

This chapter concludes by gleaning six insights from norm-setting activities in the international intellectual property regime complex. It takes the view that a deeper understanding of these activities and how they evolve within the regime complex will shed light on future negotiations for strengthening global protections for traditional knowledge and traditional cultural expressions.

title: Forecasting the Onset of Autocratization: Mass Mobilization as the Leading Early-Warning Signal
affiliations: and

detail.title: Forecasting the Onset of Autocratization: Mass Mobilization as the Leading Early-Warning Signal
detail.abstract: Democratic erosion has become the dominant mode of regime change, yet scholarship has theorized its drivers far more than it has forecast its onset. We ask which measurable antecedents best anticipate autocratization, placing candidate precursors in a common out-of-sample contest across 46 episodes in 138 countries using a five-stage framework that extracts latent democratic factors, tracks each country's trajectory through them, and separates domestic from network-transmitted erosion. Mass political mobilization emerges as the leading signal, rising for several years before onset and outranking every other channel, while government digital information control, central to recent accounts of contemporary autocratization, proves redundant once mobilization is measured. The ranking holds on average across near-optimal models and in twenty-nine of thirty measurementuncertainty draws. The framework's discrimination matches a strong gradient-boosting baseline, with AUC running from 0.82 under full-pipeline refit cross-validation to 0.93 on a 2019 temporal hold-out, so its contribution is the interpretable decomposition rather than an accuracy gain. That decomposition attributes roughly 60 percent of Hungary's recent erosion to diffusion against a third for Turkey, operating through broad global comovement rather than regional or cultural channels. As a falsifiable test, we register prospective autocratization risk rankings for 2026 through 2031 under a pre-stated evaluation rule, so the framework can be publicly scored as outcomes arrive.

reference: Banque de France Working Paper No. 1033
title: Projecting the Interests of a Dynamic Debt Portfolio: a Financial Model
affiliations: Banque de France and Banque de France

detail.title: Projecting the Interests of a Dynamic Debt Portfolio: a Financial Model

publicationDetails.detailsText: Banque de France Working Paper No. 1033
publicationDetails.journalName: Banque de France Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper presents a financial model developed to project the future interest expenses of a large set of rolling debt instruments. It aims at forecasting the financial consequences, for borrowing entities, of changes in the interest rate environment. Starting from detailed data on the current debt's maturity structure and interest rates, and given a future path for market interest rates, we simulate the progressive repayment of borrowed amounts refinanced by issuing new debt at prevailing conditions, with few structural assumptions. The model simulates the effect of variable-rate interests and inflation indexing. It can handle any joint future trajectory of outstanding amounts and interest rates, as represented by a full yield curve structure. We present two use cases: the French government marketable debt, and the aggregate debt of euro area non-financial corporations (NFC). In the former case, official publications of interest expenses provide a benchmark against which the model performance can be back-tested. The NFC use case provides evidence of a strong dependence of the interest expenses trajectory on debt structure, as the share of fixed-rate long-term debt varies widely across countries. The model quantifies the resulting differences in expense sensitivities to future interest rate changes.

title: The Throughput Problem: Why Chronic Homelessness Reached a Record High as National Homelessness Fell, and What a Capacity-Constrained System Requires
affiliations: Enfiare Inc.

detail.title: The Throughput Problem: Why Chronic Homelessness Reached a Record High as National Homelessness Fell, and What a Capacity-Constrained System Requires

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder and chief executive officer of Enfiaré Inc., a California nonprofit public benefit corporation working on homelessness. Enfiaré receives no funding contingent on the conclusions of this paper, and no component of its programmatic model is advanced or evaluated in this work. The author holds no financial interest in any organization referenced in the analysis. Readers should nonetheless weigh this affiliation when assessing the argument. The author discloses the use of AI-assisted tools in drafting portions of this manuscript. Every citation and quantitative claim was independently verified against Crossref, PubMed, publisher tables of contents, or the issuing agency's own catalog prior to submission. The author accepts full responsibility for the content.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper is a secondary analysis of publicly available federal administrative data, published point-in-time counts, and previously published peer-reviewed literature. No human subjects were recruited, enrolled, or contacted, and no individual-level or identifiable data were used.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was conducted by the author without grant support and without contract or sponsorship from any agency, foundation, or commercial entity.
declarations.clinicalTrialRegistration: Not applicable. No clinical trial was conducted.

detail.abstract:
In May 2026 the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development reported the first national decline in homelessness since 2016, with 745,652 people counted on a single night in January 2025. The same report recorded 155,750 chronically homeless individuals, the highest figure ever counted. Federal officials read the result as evidence that Housing First has failed, and the FY2026 Continuum of Care funding notice caps permanent housing at 30 percent of CoC funds, down from roughly 87 percent.

This paper argues that the data do not identify a model failure, and that they are better read as the signature of a system constrained at the point of placement rather than at the point of retention. The argument rests on an administrative figure largely absent from the public debate: 95.5 percent of people in permanent housing projects in FY2024 either retained permanent housing or exited to permanent housing. A failing intervention would show declining retention. What the data show instead is a system that keeps nearly everyone it houses while placing too few people to offset inflow. Net new dedicated capacity of 12,533 beds, together with roughly 33,000 turnover placements, proved insufficient against gross entry into chronic homelessness.

The paper states the evidence at its real magnitude, including findings unfavorable to housing-led policy. Permanent supportive housing does not reduce mortality; the long-term At Home/Chez Soi follow-up found no difference between arms. It does not reliably improve mental health or substance use outcomes. It does not pay for itself outside the highest-acuity population. Kertesz's 2009 caution regarding generalization to people with active addiction remains unresolved. Corinth's estimate of 0.04 to 0.12 fewer homeless people per additional supportive housing bed is engaged as a live challenge rather than dismissed.

Six policy recommendations follow, each labeled by strength of evidence, two of them drawn from critics of Housing First. HUD's own Family Options Study found transitional housing produced roughly a quarter of the housing effect at 2.3 times the cost of a permanent subsidy. The 2019 Council of Economic Advisers estimated a 31 percent reduction in homelessness from housing-supply deregulation, exceeding the effect of any service intervention.

title: SDM-Q: Cost-Aware Staged Decision-Making for Multi-Omics Data Classification with Deep Q-Learning
affiliations: Sichuan Normal University, Sichuan Normal University, Sichuan Normal University, Sichuan Normal University, Kennesaw State University and Kennesaw State University

detail.title: SDM-Q: Cost-Aware Staged Decision-Making for Multi-Omics Data Classification with Deep Q-Learning
detail.abstract: Multi-omics data provide complementary molecular information for disease diagnosis and subtype classification. However, acquiring complete multi-omics profiles is costly and time-consuming, whereas most existing learning methods assume full modality availability during inference, leading to redundant testing and limited clinical practicality. To address this challenge, we reformulate multi-omics classification as a cost-aware sequential decision-making problem and propose a Staged Decision-Making framework based on deep Q-learning (SDM-Q}). Specifically, the diagnostic process is modeled as a finite-horizon Markov decision process, where the currently acquired modalities define the diagnostic state and a learned action-value function determines whether to acquire additional modalities or terminate with a final prediction. To balance diagnostic performance and acquisition cost, we introduce a terminal reward formulation together with a backward stage-wise optimization strategy that improves policy consistency and training stability. Experiments on four public multi-omics datasets (BRCA, KIPAN, ROSMAP, and LGG) demonstrate that SDM-Q effectively reduces redundant modality acquisition while maintaining competitive classification performance. In particular, more than 99% of BRCA subjects and 95% of KIPAN subjects are accurately classified using only a single modality, while the average number of acquired modalities remains below two for ROSMAP and LGG. These results demonstrate the potential of SDM-Q for efficient and cost-aware multi-omics analysis in precision medicine.

title: Disinformation about Green Technologies as a Restriction of Competition
affiliations: London School of Economics - Law School

detail.title: Disinformation about Green Technologies as a Restriction of Competition

declarations.declarationOfInterest: In accordance with the ASCOLA declaration of ethics, I am happy to clarify that I have nothing to disclose.
declarations.ethicsApproval: n/a
declarations.funderStatement: n/a

detail.abstract: Disinformation-including in the energy, heating and food sectors-is an effective strategy by incumbents to prevent, hinder or delay the roll-out of green technologies. Insofar as these strategies are implemented by entities engaged in an economic activity-a category that comprises not just corporations but also, inter alia, think tanks and freelance commentators-they may fall within the scope of EU competition law. This article identifies the constituent elements of disinformation as a restriction of competition, drawing inspiration from the case law and administrative practice dealing with similar conduct. A focus on disinformation campaigns targeting green technologies would be in line with the policy themes and priorities dominating current discussions in a European context-from sustainability and resilience to competitiveness and innovation.

title: The Compounding Seat :When Prudence Pays for Vigilance

detail.title: The Compounding Seat :When Prudence Pays for Vigilance
detail.abstract: An auditing programme that models recurring internal-control failures as a no-collusion equilibrium has priced the monitor's incentives on an additive substrate, where his continuation value enters as a level - and its immediate predecessor showed that a risk-averse monitor on that substrate faces a *riskless corner*: because his safe action is to abandon the post, and an abandoned post draws a failure with certainty and a fixed floor of blame, risk aversion has nothing to price at the corner and can only buy an earlier exit. Prudence, there, cannot pay for vigilance. This paper replaces the level with a *compounding base* - a career, a licence, a partnership stake that grows while it is held and is written down when the post it sits on fails - and shows that the sign can *reverse*: on a base the monitor's own inattention can destroy, and only there, prudence pays for vigilance. The mechanism is that a monitor on a compounding base ranks outcomes by the time-average growth rate of his capital, not the ensemble average of its level, and an absorption identity - a constant-absolute-risk-aversion taste over the log-growth increment is *exactly* a constant-relative-risk-aversion growth criterion at a curvature shifted up by one, verified to machine precision - collapses the whole family of concave growth tastes into one, so the reversal is a property of compounding entering the objective and not of any functional form. The results form a ledger over two switches, seat destructibility and the criterion: wherever the seat is *insulated* the corner lottery is degenerate and prudence buys exit for every criterion (the programme's sign is preserved); the reversal requires the conjunction of a destructible seat, a criterion that prices its compounding, and a catastrophe tail heavier than a critical weight. That critical tail is characterized on a mean-preserving family that holds the seat's expected hazard fixed and varies only the shape of the loss, so the reversal is attributable to tail composition alone (the family coincides exactly at the risk-neutral pole); it has a closed form organized by a tail-shape function β(L) = −log(1−L)/L that recurs throughout, its existence is Jensen's inequality itself, and the reversal region is widest at an interior hazard budget and vanishes at both extremes. The reversal is a first-order growth-rate effect -a volatility drag the compounding forces into the objective - cleanly separated from a second-order effective-curvature drift that a level preference on a large base can mimic but the single claim does not rest on; and as the tail approaches total loss the monitor attends at any survivable charge, the penalty paradox run in reverse, with the operative survivability ceiling switching from corner-survivability under bounded adjudication lotteries to an engaged-ruin bound under unbounded ones. Geometrically the riskless corner's *trap* - the hysteresis by which vigilance once lost is hard to recover - dies on the destructible seat: sufficient prudence or tail weight converts abandonment from a first-order (hysteretic) to a second-order (continuous, reversible) transition, whose normal form on a noiseless court is a boundary cusp, distinct from the interior cusp, along a decreasing extinction boundary. But the cusp lives at skin-scale charges where adjudication risk contributes at first order to the corner's curvature even as it perturbs the levels only at second order, so under any genuine court noise the cusp relocates below the operating range, corner abandonment turns continuous, and the surviving hysteresis is an attention crash between two engaged levels detached from the corner - whose own classification is left open. A robustness analysis partitions the results by their fragility to the court's signal and finds the partition itself informative: a spine — the risk-neutral pole, the corner value, and the entire β(L) drag infrastructure - is exactly signal-free; the headline signs survive every signal structure with only second-order shifts; and exactly two things break, the amplification's endpoint and the trap's fine geometry. The analysis is confined to the monitor's decision problem, with the charge schedule exogenous and no equilibrium claim; the single-agent objects it delivers - the best-response correspondence, its regime geometry, and the comparative statics - are stated for a companion closure.

title: After the Inversion, Part I: Three Windows and the Binding Constraint of the Human-AI Transition

detail.title: After the Inversion, Part I: Three Windows and the Binding Constraint of the Human-AI Transition

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The concepts on which this paper draws, including the Asymmetric Attachment Model, the four asymmetries, the developmental staging of synthetic minds, and the account of pairing developed in the companion volume, are elaborated in full in the author’s forthcoming books, Citizen 6.0: The Psychology of Superintelligence: How the Asian Century Will Shape the Synthetic Mind and Citizen 7.0: The New Culture of Superhumans. Both books are published by CRC Press, an imprint of Taylor & Francis Group, under contract with the author, and the author gratefully acknowledges the Publisher. In keeping with the author’s publishing agreements with Taylor & Francis, this paper draws on and refers to that material as an independent scholarly article, recasting it in new prose, quoting no extended passages, reproducing none of the books’ text, and reproducing or adapting no material part of either Work. It is intended to complement, and not to compete with or substitute for, those Works, which remain the original and authoritative statement of the frameworks summarized here. This paper is the author’s own work; it is not sponsored, endorsed, commissioned, or reviewed by CRC Press or Taylor & Francis Group, and any errors are the author’s alone.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This is a conceptual paper involving no human participants, patient data, or case studies collected by the author. No ethics approval was required. All empirical findings cited derive from published studies.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was conducted independently by the author as part of the research program supporting the Citizen trilogy.

detail.abstract: The economic argument is over. Synthetic cognition is becoming cheaper than human cognition across a widening band of tasks, the crossover that Mostaque (2025) fixed in public discourse as the Intelligence Inversion, and the policy conversation has moved to what follows. The most developed answer on offer is provisioning: guarantee every person access to intelligence, in Mostaque's proposal through a universal computational entitlement, and do it within a short window before infrastructure and power lock in. This paper argues that the provisioning answer, whatever its merits, is clocked wrong. The postinversion transition is governed not by one window but by three, each closing by a different mechanism. The capability window, Mostaque's clock, closes by infrastructural and positional lock-in. The legitimacy window, formalized in the author's earlier work, closes by trust collapse, and can partially reopen at high cost. The third window, named here for the first time, is the Formation Window: the developmental period during which the first human cohorts form their foundational relational patterns with synthetic minds. Developmental science indicates that such templates, once set within a cohort, are substantially one-shot: sensitive periods close, internal working models persist, and generational imprints endure for the lifetime of the cohort. The binding constraint on the transition is therefore the minimum of the three windows, and the paper argues that the formation term binds first, which inverts the policy priority: the decisive domain of the next decade is not the provisioning of intelligence but the constitution of the human relation to it. The paper introduces a second, psychological inversion that follows the economic one, the Relational Inversion, proposes an index for tracking it, compares the three live governance architectures, provision, control, and relation, and shows that the relational architecture is already being prototyped in East Asian law and policy, from Japan's Society 5.0 to Korea's AI Framework Act. A predictions ledger states the claims in falsifiable form. Part II of this series develops the constructive program.

title: Democratic Backsliding and Allied Public Support in the US-Iran War
affiliations: Princeton University - Department of Politics, ,  and Florida State University - Department of Political Science

detail.title: Democratic Backsliding and Allied Public Support in the US-Iran War
detail.abstract: Does the democratic process at home shape allied public support for war? Bypassing domestic democratic authorization can raise concerns about transparency, accountability, restraint, and commitment to democratic norms. We argue that these concerns reduce support for the operation. We test this argument in the context of the 2026 US-Iran war using a survey experiment in Australia, Japan, South Korea, and the United Kingdom. Respondents in the main treatment condition were told that the US president initiated strikes without congressional debate or approval and that some experts considered the action unconstitutional and evidence of democratic erosion. The treatment reduced support for the strikes and for respondents' government endorsing them. Exploratory evidence indicates that a parallel expert frame that the same absence of congressional approval was constitutional did not significantly increase support. These findings suggest that backsliding into war undermines alliances from below, weakening allied public support needed for sustained military cooperation.

title: Marketization, Land Capture and the Squeezed Median Household
affiliations: UCLA Anderson

detail.title: Marketization, Land Capture and the Squeezed Median Household
detail.abstract: Suppose a paid substitute for home production is exactly as good, unit for unit, as what it replaces-no lost quality, no lost trust, no lost community. Can marketizing it alone still make the median household worse off? Yes, under a condition I derive in closed form. I build a minimal general equilibrium model, with childcare as the tractable example, showing that GDP can double while nothing real changes, and that capitalizing genuine efficiency gains into fixed urban land can leave the median household poorer even as income and GDP unambiguously rise. Richer on paper, worse off in practice.

title: The Russian-Ukrainian War: Introduction to the Symposium
affiliations: Loyola University New Orleans

detail.title: The Russian-Ukrainian War: Introduction to the Symposium
detail.abstract: Wars are economically inefficient because they destroy productive resources. Armed conflicts maim and kill people. However, wars are often credited for the development of modern nation-states. That warfare can cause a rise or decline of nations fosters interest in our understanding of its causes and consequences. The Russian-Ukrainian war is the largest international war fought on the European continent since World War II. This paper introduces a Public Choice symposium on Russia's war in Ukraine. The symposium brings together a broad range of economists and political scientists to apply the rational-choice model to the analysis of interstate war from a public choice perspective.

title: Global GDP Per Capita Growth (1961 - 2025) And Solar Activity
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Global GDP Per Capita Growth (1961 - 2025) And Solar Activity
detail.abstract: This work uses a methodological approach developed by W.S. Jevons and A.L. Chizhevsky. Years of solar cycles were numbered in the order established in solar astrophysics, grouped, and compared with average values of world GDP per capita with a one-year lag. Using the superposition of epochs method, a model with a determination coefficient of 0.9413 was obtained. The value of this coefficient in the diagram average Wolf number (independent variable)average annual growth of world GDP with a one-year lag (dependent variable) was 0.9002. To explain the obtained results, the author developed a threezone astrophysical-biochemical model. The model demonstrates that extreme solar activity-the zones of "biological depression" (Wolf number below 16) and "biological stress" (Wolf number above 156)-suppress global economic growth through hormonal imbalances (decreased serotonin and melatonin production) and subsequent pessimism. Stable growth in global per capita GDP is ensured exclusively in the "biological optimum" zone (Wolf number between 16 and 156). With a Wolf number of 123.2 in 2025, the annual growth rate of global GDP per capita in 2026 will be 1.75%. With a projected Wolf number of 91.4 in 2026, the annual growth rate of global GDP per capita in 2027 will be 2.5%. With a projected Wolf number of 10.7 in 2030, the annual growth rate of global GDP in 2031 will be-0.3%.

title: Commercial Viability of Sustainable Aviation in Regional Australia
affiliations: University of New South Wales (UNSW), University of New South Wales (UNSW) - School of Actuarial Studies and UNSW

detail.title: Commercial Viability of Sustainable Aviation in Regional Australia
detail.abstract: This paper examines the commercial viability of electric and hydrogen-powered aircraft for regional aviation in Australia under evolving carbon policy settings. Using a 25-year cost-revenue modelling framework, the study evaluates four representative route types: capital-regional, regional-regional, remote-remote, and capital-tourism connections. The analysis compares conventional aircraft with emerging sustainable platforms while accounting for fuel costs, carbon pricing, and operating economics. Results show that hydrogen and electric aircraft can be commercially viable on multiple regional routes, particularly in low-demand markets where smaller aircraft significantly reduce minimum viable passenger loads. Carbon pricing further improves the relative competitiveness of low-emission aircraft, accelerating the transition on regional corridors. Beyond emissions reductions, sustainable aviation technologies enable new routes, higher service frequency, and improved connectivity for regional and remote communities. The findings suggest that regional aviation represents a practical early adoption pathway for aviation decarbonisation, contingent on coordinated infrastructure investment and supportive policy frameworks.

title: Let the tree decide: FABART. A non-parametric factor model for nonlinear oil shock transmission
affiliations: Erasmus University Rotterdam and

detail.title: Let the tree decide: FABART. A non-parametric factor model for nonlinear oil shock transmission
detail.abstract: The question of how oil supply news shocks transmit to real activity, financial conditions, and regional labor markets is back at the center of the macroeconomic research agenda. To answer this question, we introduce the Factor Bayesian Additive Regression Tree (FABART) model, a nonlinear factor-augmented vector autoregression model, and apply it to a large U.S. macro-financial dataset with externally identified oil supply news shocks. The framework combines a large macro-financial information set with a flexible nonparametric measurement equation, allowing nonlinear transmission to emerge from the data rather than being imposed through a pre-specified functional form. We find that adverse oil supply news shocks generate stronger and more persistent contractions in real activity than the expansions associated with favorable shocks of comparable magnitude, with especially pronounced differences in industrial production, financial variables, and equity prices. Employment responses are highly heterogeneous across U.S. states, with substantially stronger contractions in manufacturing-intensive regions, while energy-producing states display partially offsetting dynamics following adverse oil supply news shocks. Across shock magnitudes, nonlinearities arise mainly between very small and moderate oil-price movements: small shocks generate weak and imprecisely estimated responses, while moderate shocks already produce economically meaningful effects on industrial production and regional employment. Larger shocks do not systematically generateproportionally stronger responses across variables and shock signs.

title: Subjective earnings and employment dynamics
affiliations: CEMFI, Yale University, University of Torino - Dipartimento di scienze economico-sociali e matematico-statistiche, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, University College London, Economics Dpt. and European Central Bank (ECB) - Directorate General Research

detail.title: Subjective earnings and employment dynamics
detail.abstract: We develop a new approach to estimating earnings, job, and employment dynamics using subjective expectations data from the NY Fed Survey of Consumer Expectations. These data provide beliefs about future earnings offers and acceptance probabilities, offering direct information on counterfactual outcomes and enabling identification under weaker assumptions. Our framework avoids biases from selection and unobserved heterogeneity that affect models using realized outcomes. First-step fixed-effects regressions identify risk, persistence, and transition effects; second-step GMM recovers the covariance structure of unobserved heterogeneities such as ability, mobility, and match quality. We find lower risk and persistence of the individual productivity component than in prior work, but greater heterogeneity in ability and match quality. Simulations show that reduced-form estimates overstate persistence and volatility on individual-level productivity due to job transitions and sorting. After accounting for heterogeneity, volatility declines and becomes flat across the earnings distribution. These results underscore the value of expectations data.

title: Application of Tax and Customs Sanctions Against Debtors in Suspension of Payment and Bankruptcy Case
affiliations: Tanjung Mas Law Office, Tarumanagara University, Tarumanagara University and Unaffiliated Author

detail.title: Application of Tax and Customs Sanctions Against Debtors in Suspension of Payment and Bankruptcy Case
detail.abstract: Debt settlement through the mechanisms of suspension of payment and bankruptcy often comes into conflict with the state's financial rights in the form of tax debts arising from trade, export and import activities. In relation to the application of administrative sanctions in the form of interest and fines, the Bankruptcy and Suspension of Payment Law states that interest and fines cannot be calculated after the debtor is declared in suspension of payment or bankrupt, while the tax and customs laws state that fines will continue to be calculated until the bill is paid in full, and coercive measures can be taken. Researchers will examine how administrative sanctions are applied to bankrupt debtors and how the mechanism for applying repressive sanctions to bankrupt debtors works? This research uses normative-empirical methods and analytical descriptive research specifications. The research results conclude that administrative sanctions for tax debts can still be applied to debtors even if they are in a state of bankruptcy can be applied to the personal assets of the taxpayer, and coercive measures can be taken. Repressive sanctions can be carried out against bankrupt debtors by officials from the Directorate General of Taxes or the Directorate General of Customs and Excise as a last resort based on the PPSP Law. The researcher provides the following suggestions: harmonization of laws and regulations is needed to prevent overlapping regulations and authorities and regulations under the law are needed to technically regulate the implementation of corporal punishment so that there is no legal vacuum.

title: Behavioral Environmental Economics
affiliations: Bocconi University and

detail.title: Behavioral Environmental Economics
detail.abstract: This paper reviews the growing field of behavioral environmental economics: the study of how cognition, beliefs, and social preferences shape sustainable behavior and the effectiveness and political feasibility of environmental policy. We synthesize recent theoretical, experimental, and empirical contributions, with emphasis on sustainable consumption, green investment, firm behavior, and political economy. We highlight design lessons and open questions for policy and research.

title: Belief Disagreement, Instability, and Uncertainty under Stochastic Recall
affiliations: University of Macau, University of Reading and National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER)

detail.title: Belief Disagreement, Instability, and Uncertainty under Stochastic Recall
detail.abstract: Expectations are typically modeled as functions of an agent’s information set. Using preregistered evidence, we show that beliefs depend instead on the information agents retrieve when forming them. Even after observing identical histories of inflation or stock returns, individuals recall different observations, and their beliefs track what they retrieve. Selective recall therefore generates disagreement, within-person belief instability, and heterogeneity in subjective uncertainty without any new information. We formalize these patterns in a parsimonious model in which agents store observed signals, retrieve each only probabilistically, and update optimally using recalled rather than objectively available information. The model yields sharp predictions for how beliefs vary with the composition of stored information, recall probabilities, and contextual cues. Large-scale experiments that hold information fixed and intervene only after exposure confirm these predictions, while survey evidence on macroeconomic and financial expectations supports their external relevance. Disagreement, instability, and uncertainty are thus structural features of belief formation rather than mere measurement error.

title: From Street Alms to Structured Welfare: Measuring Willingness to Finance Institutionalized Mistwat in Ethiopia

detail.title: From Street Alms to Structured Welfare: Measuring Willingness to Finance Institutionalized Mistwat in Ethiopia
detail.abstract: Addis Ababa has a problem that doesn't make obvious sense. People give alms constantly. The Orthodox Christian calls it Mistwat. The Muslim calls it Sadaqah. It happens at church gates, at mosque entrances, at traffic lights, on sidewalks. Millions of Birr move from hand to hand every single day. And yet the streets remain full of elderly beggars, orphaned children, and young people with nowhere to go. The giving is real. The desperation is real. They exist side by side. This paper suggests that the problem isn't the amount of giving. It's how the giving happens. Direct, person-to-person, unrecorded cash transfers keep someone alive for a day but don't change the conditions that put them on the street. The money is there. It's just fragmented beyond any ability to coordinate it or measure its effect. I propose something called the Mistwat-to-Welfare Conversion Framework. The idea is simple: take the informal giving that already exists and channel it into structured institutions-elderly care homes, orphanages, youth training centers-without losing the human connection that makes almsgiving meaningful in the first place. I use a contingent valuation survey design with 600 households across three income groups in Addis Ababa to measure how much people would be willing to contribute to a National Dignity Fund. The study isn't just about measuring willingness to pay. It's about whether trust in institutions can substitute for the warm-glow people get from handing coins directly to a beggar. The paper also proposes a governance model drawn from Zakat systems in Malaysia and Indonesia, Jewish tzedakah traditions, Christian tithing structures, and Ethiopia's own Iddir and Iqub associations. And it includes safeguards-local community councils, mandatory donor-recipient contact, dignity-before-efficiency principles-to prevent the whole thing from becoming another cold bureaucracy. This is a pre-analysis plan. The actual data hasn't been collected yet. The full plan will be registered on OSF before fieldwork begins.

title: Taxing Cross-Border Services
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF) - Fiscal Affairs Department, International Monetary Fund (IMF), , , International Monetary Fund (IMF) - Fiscal and Financial Law Unit, International Monetary Fund (IMF),  and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Taxing Cross-Border Services
detail.abstract: Faced with the limitations of existing tax frameworks for cross-border trade in services — particularly the lack of taxing rights over certain income from highly digital business models and the continuing scope for profit shifting through payments for cross-border services — countries and scholars have adopted or proposed a wide range of tax measures. This paper brings these measures together in a coherent framework and examines them from both an economic and a legal perspective. It documents how cross-border services trade has grown, become more digital in composition, and become increasingly concentrated across sectors, firms, and jurisdictions. It then develops a comparative synthesis covering destination-based consumption taxes such as VAT, gross-revenue taxes — notably digital services taxes — as well as income-based instruments such as nexus and withholding rules, and anti-avoidance rules aimed at limiting profit shifting through deductible cross-border payments. The paper argues that the economic incidence of each instrument is central to policy assessment and that evaluating these instruments in isolation obscures their interaction. Its main conclusion is that broader reliance on destination-based taxation can address many of the core problems raised by digitalized services trade more effectively than narrower, more distortionary alternatives.

title: The Price of Regulatory Risk in Housing Markets: Evidence from Berlin
affiliations: Ifo Institute, ifo Institute – Leibniz Institute for Economic Research at the University of Munich, Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU) - ifo Institute (Leibniz Institute for Economic Research at the University of Munich), ifo Institute and Ifo Institute

detail.title: The Price of Regulatory Risk in Housing Markets: Evidence from Berlin
detail.abstract: We study how regulatory risk affects housing markets in the aftermath of rent control. Our setting is Berlin, where a stringent rent cap introduced in 2020 was repealed in 2021, but was followed by continued political debate over expropriation of housing companies and further intervention. Using micro-level listing data and a hedonic difference-in-differences design comparing Berlin to other major German cities, we show that Berlin’s price-rent ratio remained 10–15 percent below its pre-intervention trend three years after repeal. To interpret this persistence, we develop a simple model in which institutional investors face greater exposure to future regulation. The model predicts lower asset prices, reduced institutional ownership, and partial crowding-in of private investors. Consistent with these predictions, we document a sharp rise in housing policy uncertainty after repeal and show that large housing companies reduced their Berlin portfolios, accepted lower sale prices, and sharply cut construction activity. The results imply that credible threats of future intervention can depress housing valuations and reshape market structure even in the absence of binding regulation.

title: Do Markets Deliver? Competition and Choice in European Healthcare Markets
affiliations: Imperial College London Business School

detail.title: Do Markets Deliver? Competition and Choice in European Healthcare Markets
detail.abstract: In the last two decades European policy makers have sought to increase the use of market mechanisms in the delivery of healthcare. These reforms introduce competition and choice into previously heavily constrained environments. This leads to a set of interesting economic issues that have been addressed in a range of papers, both theoretical and empirical. This paper examines whether this popular reform model has resulted in improvements in outcomes for patients and/or taxpayers. It synthesises the existing economic analyses, highlights what is known and what is not, and signals potential next steps for economic research.

title: Trust but Verify: Benchmarking Gallup World Poll Employment Data Against the EU-Labour Force Survey
affiliations: and

detail.title: Trust but Verify: Benchmarking Gallup World Poll Employment Data Against the EU-Labour Force Survey
detail.abstract: The Gallup World Poll (GWP) links internationally comparable measures of well-being and attitudes to a short labour-market module. We benchmark its employment and hours variables against EU Labour Force Survey (EU LFS) microdata in available European country-years from 2009 to 2023. Under a broad GWP definition that includes both part-time categories, the average country-level GWP-EU LFS employment-rate gap is approximately -1.0 percentage point. The pooled Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition yields a total gap of -0.85 points: observable composition accounts for -0.97 points and the unexplained component is 0.12 points, with a standard error of 1.99 points. This aggregate result masks country and demographic heterogeneity. A narrow definition that excludes part-time work understates employment by roughly 10-20 points. For hours, the GWP mean is 40.18 hours per week, compared with 37.41 in the EU LFS. Demographic reweighting reduces the aggregate difference from 2.77 to 1.99 hours, while group-specific reweighting raises each country-group difference by 0.11 to 0.58 hour. Hours reports generally require more recall and aggregation than binary employment status. The GWP limits this burden by anchoring employment to the preceding seven days and recording total weekly hours in five intervals. The resulting variable provides a common interval-based measure of work intensity; exact mean levels depend on the values assigned to those intervals.

title:
Quiet Opportunism: 
Automation Threat and the Silencing of Employee Voice
affiliations: Institute of Financial Studies, Southwestern University of Finance and Economics

detail.title:
Quiet Opportunism: 
Automation Threat and the Silencing of Employee Voice

keywords: Opportunistic Insider Trading JEL Classification: G14

detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of automation potential on managerial opportunism. To this end, we exploit the stringent reporting deadline of 8-K filings relative to 10-K filings to disentangle an unfiltered reflection of the firm's underlying reality from strategic managerial tone management. We find that high automation potential is associated with more negative tone in both 8-K and 10-K filings. However, 10-K filings uniquely exhibit an increase in confident language and a decrease in litigation-related words, consistent with strategic tone management. We show that firms with greater automation potential exhibit a lower public information share in stock prices and higher idiosyncratic risk, providing evidence that the corporate information environment becomes less informative. We further document that automation potential is associated with higher executive compensation and greater opportunistic insider sales intensity, suggesting that managers exploit this less informative environment for their private benefits. Overall, we provide new evidence in the literature that automation potential carries an unintended consequence: it may create a governance vacuum by eroding employee voice, enabling a form of quiet opportunism that remains elusive to external monitors.

title: Expert Inflation Preferences and the Evaluation of Monetary Policy
affiliations: , ETH Zürich - Department of Management, Technology, and Economics (D-MTEC) and

detail.title: Expert Inflation Preferences and the Evaluation of Monetary Policy
detail.abstract: What inflation rate should central banks target? Using two global surveys, we provide evidence on inflation preferences among economic experts—the group whose models and judgments inform monetary policy. We document that, although experts’ preferred inflation rates are centered on central-bank targets, roughly half of them deviate (symmetrically) from the target. Cross-expert heterogeneity in preferences is driven by (i) beliefs about the costs of disinflation, (ii) normative views on the relative importance of different central bank objectives, and (iii) inflation narratives. Finally, we show that experts’ preferences influence their evaluations of monetary policy decisions, suggesting that experts’ preferences are likely to matter for policymaking.

title: A Regressive Shock? The Distributional Consequences of Middle East Conflict-Driven Inflation for German Households
affiliations: Universidad Loyola Andalucía,  and

detail.title: A Regressive Shock? The Distributional Consequences of Middle East Conflict-Driven Inflation for German Households
detail.abstract: The escalation of the conflict in the Middle East in late February 2026 led to a sharp upward revision in inflation forecasts for Germany, which we attribute primarily to the conflict itself. Using microsimulation methods adapted to simulate a commodity price change, we translate this forecast revision into upper bounds on household-specific purchasing-power losses via a compensating variation approach, distinguishing the loss recovered through consumption taxes from the full loss including the pre-tax transfer to producers. Both measures are sizeable and regressive: in 2026, the average household loses 0.25% of income through the tax channel and 1.15% under the full measure, with bottom-decile losses of 0.63% and 2.87% against 0.12% and 0.65% for the top decile. The Gini coefficient rises by up to 0.14 points, and elderly households are disproportionately affected. Our results show that a supply-side shock originating outside Europe can have a sizeable and unequal impact on household living standards.

title: Fiscal Sustainability and Sovereign Risk Pricing: Evidence from Time-Varying Fiscal Reaction
affiliations: Bielefeld University - Department of Business Administration and Economics

detail.title: Fiscal Sustainability and Sovereign Risk Pricing: Evidence from Time-Varying Fiscal Reaction
detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether fiscal sustainability is priced in sovereign bond markets. For this purpose, we construct a standard measure of fiscal sustainability for 21 EU countries, namely, a time-varying fiscal reaction coefficient measuring the response of the cyclically adjusted primary balance to lagged debt. Next, we examine the response of sovereign yield spreads and credit default swap (CDS) to our fiscal sustainability parameter within a panel data framework. The results from static and dynamic linear panel models do not reveal statistically significant effects of fiscal sustainability on sovereign risk premia. However, nonlinear regime-switching estimations indicate significant threshold effects. In particular, fiscal sustainability exerts a significant effect on sovereign bond spreads once public debt exceeds a threshold of approximately 60% of GDP. The evidence for CDS spreads is mixed. For a subsumple of Eurozone group of countries, the threshold effect is more pronounced. Overall, the findings suggest that sovereign debt markets become more sensitive to fiscal sustainability considerations when public debt levels exceed the Maastricht threshold.

title:
Mapping Diplomatic Representation in Europe, 1648-1715 
New Data from the Repertorium der diplomatischen Vertreter
affiliations: University of Gothenburg - Department of Political Science

detail.title:
Mapping Diplomatic Representation in Europe, 1648-1715 
New Data from the Repertorium der diplomatischen Vertreter
detail.abstract: This paper introduces new data on diplomatic representation in Europe between 1648 and 1715, drawn from Band I of the Repertorium der diplomatischen Vertreter aller Länder. The data comprise 13,344 diplomatic missions, exchanged among 141 sending and 201 receiving polities, and 8,852 individual representatives. The paper describes the source and coding procedure, assesses the quality and limits of the data, and reports patterns in participation, rank, and mission duration. In an illustrative application, I use the data to examine diplomatic continuity across ruler successions, with findings suggesting that individual appointments remained tied to the person of the ruler even as the relationships they served proved durable. The dataset will be useful for research on recognition and membership in the states system, status and hierarchy among polities, and the formation of the early modern state. Data collection will continue, and Bands II and III will extend the series to 1815.

title: Factory Parents, Classroom Outcomes: Occupational Networks and Peer Effects in Education

detail.title: Factory Parents, Classroom Outcomes: Occupational Networks and Peer Effects in Education
detail.abstract: We study how exposure to classmates from manufacturing and production worker families affects academic achievement in urban Chinese middle schools. Exploiting the random assignment of students to classrooms within school-grade cohorts in the China Education Panel Survey (CEPS), we find that a ten-percentage-point increase in the share of peers with production worker parents reduces standardized academic scores by approximately 0.21 standard deviations. The effect is robust and statistically significant across all specifications, and present for all three core subjects (mathematics, Chinese language, and English). We investigate mechanisms using rich parent questionnaire data. Exposure to the working-class peer families significantly reduces other parents' engagement with children's friendship networks, particularly the inter-family social connections and peer-relationship communication that require bridging social capital, as well as school discussion frequency, parental confidence in children's academic futures, and parent-initiated teacher contact. Parents in classrooms with more working-class families also report systematically lower evaluations of the educational environment. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that the effect is stronger for students from non-low-income families, consistent with higher initial social capital endowments amplifying the cost of peer-composition shifts. Falsification tests using business and service sector workers, who share comparable earnings and education levels but work in more socially interactive occupations, yield uniformly null effects across all outcomes. These findings reveal how occupational class composition of the classroom shapes the parental social capital networks that support children's education, with implications for school integration policies and class-based educational inequality in rapidly industrializing economies.

title: Inside the Black Box: Class Environment and Performance in Chinese Middle Schools

detail.title: Inside the Black Box: Class Environment and Performance in Chinese Middle Schools
detail.abstract: This paper jointly examines three theoretically distinct dimensions of classroom social environment-teacher-student relationship quality, peer academic norms, and peer relationship quality-and their effects on student academic achievement. Using two waves of the China Education Panel Survey (CEPS), a nationally representative panel of 7,653 middleschool students across 112 schools (2013-2015), we estimate value-added models with school fixed effects, rich baseline controls, and multiple robustness specifications. A one-standarddeviation improvement in teacher-student relationship quality predicts a 0.045-SD gain in composite academic achievement, stable across class fixed effects, change-in-environment, and ability-tracking subsamples. A one-SD improvement in peer academic norms predicts a 0.049-SD gain, confirmed by Double Machine Learning. Peer relationship quality is null in the full model; psychological safety promotes achievement while social cohesion modestly crowds out academic effort through social time substitution. Peer norm effects are largest for students with low prior ability and rural household registration, consistent with academically oriented peer norms functioning as a compensating resource for students with fewer external academic supports. Mechanism analysis shows that within teacher-student quality, instructional engagement dominates emotional support in a 1.7-to-1 ratio; within peer norms, academic values exert more than twice the effect of behavioral effort conformity, favoring an aspirational over a conformity-based interpretation of peer influence. We develop a novel reverse-causality falsification test exploiting within-index heterogeneity in sensitivity to performance feedback.

title: The Scandinavian Greenium: Sector Asymmetry and Currency Effects in Green Bond Pricing
affiliations: Grenoble Ecole de Management, Grenoble Ecole de Management, Grenoble Ecole de Management and

detail.title: The Scandinavian Greenium: Sector Asymmetry and Currency Effects in Green Bond Pricing

declarations.declarationOfInterest: All authors declare that they have no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This article does not contain any studies with human participants or animals performed by any of the authors.
declarations.funderStatement: The authors received no financial support for the research, authorship, and/or publication of this article.

detail.abstract: Scandinavian bond markets are among the world's most sustainability-oriented, yet evidence on their green bond pricing remains limited. Using 55,900 bond-month observations for 1,883 bonds issued in Norway, Sweden, and Denmark between 2018 and 2025, we examine whether the greenium is a broad market feature or concentrated in specific segments. We find a modest market-wide greenium of about 6 basis points, but this average masks a sharp sector asymmetry: government green bonds trade at a persistent 9 to 16 basis point yield discount, while corporate green bonds show no significant greenium. We also show that omitting currency effects inflates the estimated greenium to 26 basis points. These findings suggest that the Scandinavian greenium is concentrated in government bonds and that currency composition is a key methodological issue in multi-currency green bond markets.

title: The Insurance Gap: Liability Frameworks for Ontological Attacks on Clinical AI
affiliations: Martin-Luther-University Halle-Wittenberg and

detail.title: The Insurance Gap: Liability Frameworks for Ontological Attacks on Clinical AI
detail.abstract: The European Union's AI Act and the European Health Data Space regulate the technical compliance and data quality of clinical artificial intelligence systems, but neither addresses liability for a distinct category of attack: the ontological attack, in which adversarial inputs corrupt the semantic layer of clinical terminology systems rather than their technical infrastructure. Existing cyber-insurance products cover the confidentiality, integrity, and availability triad but not the case in which data is technically intact while semantically corrupted. Drawing on an adversarial ontology threat taxonomy recently formalised in the clinical AI literature (Stummer 2026), we map six attack categories to existing insurance product classes, identify two categories (terminology poisoning and semantic drift induction) for which no coverage exists, and provide a Fermi estimate of the uninsured annual exposure in the European Union of approximately EUR 2 to 5 billion, with a central estimate of EUR 3 billion. We propose a three-layer liability framework distinguishing technical, semantic, and ontological damage, discuss moral hazard and adverse selection implications, and analyse three regulatory pathways: soft-law guidance from the European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority, amendment of Article 15 of the AI Act to require liability cover for high-risk clinical AI systems, and market-led standardisation through a Lloyd's or Munich Re pilot product. Limitations: the market-size estimate is Fermi-anchored rather than actuarial; documented ontological-attack incident data do not yet exist; the regulatory focus is the European Union, with United States and Asian markets analysed only secondarily; the proposed insurance products are conceptual and require dedicated actuarial modelling before underwriting feasibility can be assessed.

title: First They Came for the Others: A Theory of Divide-and-Conquer
affiliations: Columbia University, Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) and Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Economics

detail.title: First They Came for the Others: A Theory of Divide-and-Conquer
detail.abstract: Divide-and-conquer tactics often succeed not through mechanical coordination failures, but through epistemic friction regarding an aggressor's underlying intent. When an attacker strikes a first target, bystanders must infer whether the assault represents a localized grievance or a systemic campaign. If the attack is rationally interpreted as particularized, bystanders abstain, prompting the isolated victim to surrender. We demonstrate how higher attack costs and lower correlation between victims' fates facilitate this division. We then study how behavioral responses, rhetoric, treaty commitments, and downstream defense networks modify this inference.

title: Cryonic Trusts and the Architecture of Indefinite Control
affiliations: The University of Georgia

detail.title: Cryonic Trusts and the Architecture of Indefinite Control
detail.abstract: Thousands of Americans have been cryonically frozen or have arranged to be frozen after death in hopes that they will one day be revived. Reanimation remains scientifically impossible, but estate planning has not treated that impossibility as a reason to wait. The cryotrust exists to spare a successfully revived decedent the indignity of being resurrected and poor by placing wealth in storage: a modest $1 million investment, compounded for a century with no distributions and no transfer tax to slow it down, emerges worth over $2 billion, waiting for a settlor who may never return to claim it. This Article argues that the cryotrust is not a futuristic curiosity but a logical, doctrinally ordinary product of a trust law that has spent decades hollowing out the safeguards meant to keep it tethered to living people and finite time. Drawing on the concepts of reification and tilt, the Article argues that cryotrusts are troubling precisely because they are unremarkable: the modern dynasty trust, the asset protection trust, and the offshore trust all share the same architecture, and all depend upon treating a legal form as a neutral "thing" rather than a set of contestable social and distributive choices. The cryotrust is offered here as a diagnostic case study, not a call to regulate cryonics, but rather an argument that the proper unit of analysis is the system of trust law that produced this result, not any single statute. The Article closes with a menu of reforms designed to restore temporal and beneficiary-based limits without sacrificing the flexibility that makes trust law valuable.

title: Legal Risk Management in M&A Transactions
affiliations: O.P. Jindal Global University - Jindal Global Law School

detail.title: Legal Risk Management in M&A Transactions
detail.abstract: As modern economic complexity increases, effective risk management dictates the success of corporate restructuring. This dissertation examines critical legal risks encountered during the Mergers and Acquisitions (M&A) process and outlines strategic methods to mitigate or prevent them. It specifically addresses the rising threat of social media on transaction confidentiality, evaluating how well-crafted Non-Disclosure Agreements (NDAs) can control unauthorized diligence and public leaks. Furthermore, the study analyzes the legal and structural challenges associated with cross-border M&A deals under the Indian regulatory framework—including merger control thresholds and compliance liabilities—supported by practical insights from an in-house counsel interview and notable corporate case studies. Identifying and tracking these transaction vulnerabilities in a timely manner ultimately enables executives to execute robust corporate decisions and safeguard business assets.

title: AI Advice Suppresses People's Willingness to Say, "I Don't Know", Even When the Advice Is Wrong and Accuracy is Incentivized
affiliations: Sorbonne University - École Normale Supérieure, University of Rome Sapienza and Università degli Studi di Milano-Bicocca - Department of Psychology

detail.title: AI Advice Suppresses People's Willingness to Say, "I Don't Know", Even When the Advice Is Wrong and Accuracy is Incentivized

declarations.ethicsApproval: This work has been approved by the Committee for Research Evaluation (CRIP) of the University of Milan-Bicocca, Psychology Department.

detail.abstract: Knowing when to say "I don't know" is fundamental to human judgment, yet AI assistants offer a fluent answer to almost any question. In five experiments (N = 3,132; four preregistered, one direct replication), participants answered difficult questions and could always decline to respond. We engineered the questions so that AI advice was wrong, separating AI use from its accuracy. Merely having access to AI nearly eliminated participants' willingness to suspend judgment, and this held whether the advice was actively requested or simply displayed. Consequently, participants answered more questions but were correct about a third as often as when AI was unavailable-yet their confidence nearly doubled. Incentivizing accuracy and penalizing inaccuracy led participants to seek and follow AI advice less, answer more accurately, and suspend judgment more often, though still far less than when AI was unavailable. As AI suggestions grow ubiquitous and unsolicited, they may not simply affect answer accuracy; they may even alter the metacognitive threshold at which people decide whether they know enough to answer.

title: Know the Economy, not the Data Lake: Country Structure and the Right Number of Indicators in a GDP Nowcast
affiliations: and

detail.title: Know the Economy, not the Data Lake: Country Structure and the Right Number of Indicators in a GDP Nowcast
detail.abstract: How many indicators should a GDP nowcast use, and how should that number be chosen? A common answer is to add every available series and let a factor model or a machine-learning method separate signal from noise. We argue that this misplaces the effort for most economies. The number of indicators that can help is bounded by how many distinct sources of cyclical signal an economy generates, which is a feature of its structure rather than of the available data. We write the choice as a bias-variance trade-off. The accuracy-maximising count k * rises with the sample length and with the number of orthogonal signal dimensions, and it falls with volatility, so less-diversified economies nowcast best with fewer indicators. We test this on twelve economies. Each faces the same harmonised menu of headline indicators, informed by the blocks that published flagship nowcasts use, over a common 2000 to 2026 out-of-sample window. The optimum is smaller in emerging economies (mean 3.2 against 6.4; p = 0.026), and it is explained by economic complexity (0.61) rather than income (0.35, not significant). Norway is the identifying case. It is rich but resource-concentrated, and its optimum sits with the emerging economies, where complexity predicts it and income does not.

title: Dynamic Income-Oriented Pension Investment Model
affiliations: Comenius University - Faculty of Mathematics, Physics and Informatics; Department of Applied Mathematics and Statistics

detail.title: Dynamic Income-Oriented Pension Investment Model
detail.abstract: We present a stochastic dynamic model of retirement saving with maximization of the expected utility of pension income. In contrast to traditional models, we change the paradigm from value-oriented to income-oriented. The model uses SeLFIES (Standard-of-Living Forward-starting Income-only Securities) as risk-free assets. SeLFIES has a defined stream of payments starting at retirement for a defined period. Payments are indexed by consumption per capita or inflation from the time of issuance. The paradigm change from value-oriented to income-oriented causes a change in the risk ranking of assets. Government bonds with longer maturities are less risky assets compared to those with shorter maturities. We present the optimal level of savings in the form of a certainty equivalent and an internal rate of return of the certainty equivalent. In addition, we calculate the time evolution of the optimal allocation of investments into different types of assets. Optimal saving strategies deliver satisfactory replacement rates.

title: Does Inequality Reduce Native Bias? Evidence from a Survey Experiment
affiliations: CMCC - Centro Euro-Mediterraneo sui Cambiamenti Climatici, Università degli Studi di Milano, University of Pavia and University of Milan - University of Milan

detail.title: Does Inequality Reduce Native Bias? Evidence from a Survey Experiment

declarations.ethicsApproval: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the University of Milano (Parere 59/24).

detail.abstract: This paper experimentally examines whether native bias-the tendency to favor compatriots over foreigners-is affected by exposure to inequality. We study donation behavior in a representative sample of 2,382 Italian respondents who allocated part of their participation bonus to Italians and immigrants living in poverty in Italy. We vary (i) the size of the bonus, (ii) the rule used to assign the bonus to each participantrandom versus identity-based, and (iii) whether participants are informed about the bonuses received by others. We find a pronounced native bias in giving. However, making inequality salient by revealing unequal bonus allocations reduces this bias, but only among respondents who are disadvantaged by the allocation. We also find that the effect of being a victim of inequality does not depend on the source of the inequality.

title: Geopolitical Shocks and Aid Retrenchment in a Nascent State

detail.title: Geopolitical Shocks and Aid Retrenchment in a Nascent State
detail.abstract: Somalia entered 2026 under two compounding external shocks, a historic contraction in foreign assistance and the economic spillovers of intensifying geopolitical rivalry and regional conflict. This paper examines how these shocks are transmitted through a fragile, import-dependent economy and what they imply for fiscal space. United States disbursements fell to US$487.2 million in 2025, 42.3 per cent below the 2020-2024 annual average, within a wider decline in official development assistance. Regional conflict has simultaneously raised freight, insurance and energy costs along the Red Sea and Gulf corridors. Combined traffic at Somalia's four main ports fell 15.4 per cent below its prior-year benchmark in the first quarter of 2026, fuel prices in Mogadishu rose from about US$0.60 to US$1.50 per litre after the February 2026 escalation, and year-on-year inflation returned to an estimated 5.5-6.8 per cent. Scenario estimates indicate that aid shocks equivalent to 3.0-4.6 per cent of GDP could reduce growth by 0.8-1.4 percentage points and domestic revenue by US$8-14 million, while trade-linked taxes-56.5 per cent of tax collections in FY2025-remain directly exposed to shipping disruption. Revenue execution fell to 69.1 per cent of budget in FY2025 and adjustment was concentrated in social benefits and capital spending.
