This study addresses this debate for the United States by: 1) synthesizing key institutional and social constraints that limit renewable deployment, including local opposition, fragmented siting and zoning regimes, and persistent permitting bottlenecks; 2) summarizing and evaluating dual-use land strategies that minimize land impacts and link them to associated energy and cost trade-offs, highlighting where economic benefits could offset some social acceptance concerns; and 3) proposing siting priorities that, in abstraction from current social and policy resistance, would allow a 100% renewable US energy system and quantifying the associated land requirements and system costs under relaxed institutional constraints. This framework clarifies, through country-specific land-cover, cost, and siting assumptions, how governance and social-acceptance barriers, rather than physical limits, constrain deployment. Results indicate that, conditional on substantially reducing regulatory and social barriers, the United States could develop a 100% renewable infrastructure with minimal impact on undisturbed land (0.6%) and lower total energy costs (19% reduction) than current fossil fuel-based systems. These findings demonstrate that neither land availability nor cost is the binding constraint on a US renewable transition. Rather, the main barriers lie in governance and social acceptance.

title: Dual Leviathan: Domestic Datafication and the Sanctioned Governance Vacuum in Iran's Digital Ecosystem

detail.title: Dual Leviathan: Domestic Datafication and the Sanctioned Governance Vacuum in Iran's Digital Ecosystem
detail.abstract: Iran presents a sui generis problem for comparative digital constitutionalism. Two structural conditions-the Islamic Republic's security-sovereignty governance architecture and the extraterritorial reach of United States sanctions law-generate what this article terms the dual Leviathan: a configuration in which domestic platforms operate under a governance framework that resolves state security concerns while leaving commercial datafication structurally unregulated, while foreign platforms enjoy structural immunity from Iranian jurisdiction because the very commercial relationships that generate regulatory leverage elsewhere are legally prohibited by OFAC. Drawing on corpus analysis of 131 Khamenei speeches, 200+ HCC decrees, ministerial discourse across three ICT ministerial eras, browser-based technical inspection of platform tracking architectures, and 710 judicial cases from the Edaalate Ali leaked court records, this article maps both configurations. It argues that the absent Leviathan-a platform legally present for end-users but commercially absent and structurally unreachable-is not a product of platform choice but a structural effect of sanctions bifurcation, and that this configuration has no adequate conceptual framework in the existing digital constitutionalism literature. The article proposes sanctions-mediated regulatory vacancy as a conceptual supplement to the digital constitutionalism toolkit, with implications for how platform accountability is theorised in non-Western jurisdictions subject to extraterritorial economic sanctions.

title: The Structural Conditions of Off-Earth Expansion: From Cislunar Presence to Self-Replicating Production

detail.title: The Structural Conditions of Off-Earth Expansion: From Cislunar Presence to Self-Replicating Production

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is an independent geostrategic theorist with no institutional, commercial, or financial relationship bearing on this study. The author declares no competing interests. The analysis is the author's own independent scholarly work and does not represent the position of any institution.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper is a theoretical and analytical study in geostrategy and international political economy. It involves no human or animal participants, no clinical or experimental data, and no personal data. Ethics approval is therefore not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or funding from any agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. It was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: This paper analyzes off-Earth expansion in two stages. The first is the threshold at which an existing global flow system sustains production beyond its terrestrial operating space. The second is the threshold at which an off-Earth node produces not only its own consumption goods but the machines of the next node. Part One establishes the structural conditions of the first threshold: why an open three-dimensional volume makes expansion positive-sum rather than zero-sum; how the basis of power has shifted across recorded history, with space presence as the current transition; why a space-capable great power must integrate three pillars, launch, energy, and compute, rather than possess any one of them; why three-power coordination, though incentivized by an open prize, remains structurally unstable; and how expedition gives way to persistent presence and then to a production node that closes a material loop off Earth. Part Two analyzes the second threshold, self-replicating production, using the closure ratio, the fraction of a new node's mass and capability produced from local material, as its load-bearing metric. It traces why information closes first and matter last, why the binding constraint is the local manufacture of motors and electronics rather than the design, and why the architecture is machine-first, the light delay placing the decision at the edge. An appendix derives how the geometry of flow itself transforms, from a continuous terrestrial field into a high-latency network of surface-nodes, when the system extends into the Solar System. Throughout, the argument is structural and conditional, not predictive: it specifies what must hold, not what will occur.

title: Human in the Loop, Machine in the Pipeline: An Evidence Synthesis of Generative AI Productivity, Verification Overhead, and Repository-Scale Risk in Software Engineering

detail.title: Human in the Loop, Machine in the Pipeline: An Evidence Synthesis of Generative AI Productivity, Verification Overhead, and Repository-Scale Risk in Software Engineering

declarations.declarationOfInterest: "The author declares that there are no financial or personal relationships with other people or organizations that could inappropriately influence or bias this work."
declarations.ethicsApproval: "This study does not involve any human participants, patients, or animals. All research was conducted using open-source tools and publicly available datasets, and therefore ethical approval was not required."
declarations.funderStatement: "This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. It was entirely self-funded by the author."

detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has rapidly moved from experimental code completion to an increasingly integrated component of software development workflows. However, evidence concerning its effect on engineering productivity remains heterogeneous. Controlled experiments have reported substantial acceleration on bounded implementation tasks, whereas recent field experiments involving experienced developers working in familiar repositories have observed productivity slowdowns under AI-assisted conditions. At the same time, developer surveys and security studies identify persistent concerns regarding output accuracy, debugging effort, insecure code, and the verification of machine-generated changes. This paper presents a structured evidence synthesis of empirical research on generative AI in software engineering. We examine four questions: how AI assistance affects developer productivity; why reported productivity effects differ across experimental settings; what evidence exists regarding verification, security, and repository-scale limitations; and what engineering controls follow from the combined evidence. The synthesis indicates that the productivity effect of AI coding assistance is strongly context dependent. Benefits are most consistently observed for bounded and well-specified generation tasks, while evidence from mature repositories highlights the importance of implicit requirements, repository familiarity, and human validation. Security studies further demonstrate that functional plausibility does not guarantee secure implementation. Based on the synthesized evidence, we propose Continuous Verification and Sandboxing (CVS), a reference architecture that places isolated execution, static analysis, security scanning, and test-based evaluation between machine generation and human peer review. CVS is presented as an evidence-derived design implication rather than an empirically validated intervention. We conclude that generative AI should be evaluated as part of a socio-technical software delivery pipeline in which generation cost, verification cost, and integration risk are measured jointly.

title: Who Competes for Whom? Monopsony in Ability-Segregated Labor Markets

detail.title: Who Competes for Whom? Monopsony in Ability-Segregated Labor Markets
detail.abstract: I develop a general-equilibrium oligopsony model in which firms differ in their demand for worker ability, generating worker-specific monopsony power. Taking the model to matched employer–employee data for Italy and Germany reveals ability segregation that localizes competition: firms compete most intensely with similar firms targeting the same ability segment. In the calibrated model, monopsony power and welfare losses are largest for low- and high- ability workers, who face fewer effective employers. Output losses are modest relative to standard quantitative benchmarks. Labor-market power amplifies wage inequality because wider between-market wage dispersion outweighs compressed assortative matching and top wages.

title: Defaulting to the State: Accountability Concerns, Instrument Uncertainty, and Demand for AI Regulation
affiliations: University of Barcelona, Oxford University and

detail.title: Defaulting to the State: Accountability Concerns, Instrument Uncertainty, and Demand for AI Regulation
detail.abstract: Recent surveys reveal strong public support for stringent regulation of AI, yet we still know little about what this demand means for citizens. We argue that mass support for strict AI regulation partly reflects a combination of concerns about who is accountable for AI-related risks and lack of knowledge about how oversight could be organized. Using novel data from six countries that together account for 75% of world investment in AI, we find broad support for government oversight across diverse AI applications, yet open-ended responses reveal that only a minority connect this support to specific policy instruments. Experimental evidence shows that learning about non-ban oversight mechanisms progressively softens demands, suggesting that what citizens demand is credible governance in a domain where the available instruments remain poorly understood. To conclude, we discuss the implications of our findings for the analysis of public opinion in new or technical policy domains.

title: The Judicial Sidelining of Cost-Benefit Analysis
affiliations: University of Connecticut - School of Law

detail.title: The Judicial Sidelining of Cost-Benefit Analysis
detail.abstract:
Just over a decade ago, the Supreme Court announced in Michigan v. EPA that “no regulation is ‘appropriate’ if it does significantly more harm than good.” Cass Sunstein hailed the decision as a “ringing endorsement of cost-benefit analysis by government agencies.” But the Court’s enthusiasm for CBA as a regulatory lodestar appears to have been short-lived. Though Michigan remains good law, the Court has since made other doctrinal changes that will indirectly but systemically impede agencies’ pursuit of the net-benefit-maximizing regulatory outcomes that CBA deems most desirable.

Specifically, this Article argues that the Court’s repudiation of Chevron deference in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo renders CBA formally irrelevant to many of an agency’s decisions on statutory implementation. Whereas agencies could previously interpret cryptic Congressional commands with an eye toward efficiency, they must now focus on predicting what a reviewing court will deem the “single, best meaning” of any ambiguous statutory term or phrase. And even where the statute is “best” read as granting the agency discretion to make a CBA-informed policy choice, the major questions doctrine announced in West Virginia v. EPA may inefficiently constrain the exercise of that discretion. Why? Because the doctrine encourages judicial skepticism of costly and novel rules, even when they offer greater net benefits than more modest and familiar alternatives.

All of this is welcome news to the Trump administration, which hopes to rescind many existing regulations that were found net beneficial when initially promulgated. Concededly discretionary repeals of such rules would be vulnerable to challenge under Michigan, on the theory that their rescission unreasonably does more harm (in the form of forgone regulatory benefits) than good (in the form of avoided compliance costs). But Loper Bright and West Virginia make it easier to characterize repeals as mandatory—that is, to argue that existing rules are unlawful and must be scrapped, no matter the consequences. The administration has, accordingly, made the cases central to the deregulatory initiatives of its second term.

title: Trump's Tariffs and Trade Resilience: A Comparative PPML Analysis of Jordan and Egypt's Export performance
affiliations: Future University in Egypt FUE and Mohammed Bin Rashid School of Government

detail.title: Trump's Tariffs and Trade Resilience: A Comparative PPML Analysis of Jordan and Egypt's Export performance
detail.abstract: The study investigates the differential impact of U.S. tariffs imposed under President Donald Trump (2017–2021 and 2025) on the export performance of Jordan and Egypt—two MENA economies with divergent trade structures, market dependencies, and policy regimes. Employing a structural gravity model estimated via Poisson Pseudo-Maximum Likelihood (PPML) with high dimensional fixed effects (exporter-year and importer-year), real effective exchange rates, and the World Uncertainty Index over the period 2015–2025, we find that a one-percentage-point increase in the U.S. tariff rate reduces Egyptian exports by 23.8% and Jordanian exports by 25.9%. Despite Jordan’s preferential access under the U.S.–Jordan Free Trade Agreement (2001), the interaction term is statistically insignificant, indicating that 2025 reciprocal tariffs effectively erode FTA benefits. Real effective exchange rate appreciation significantly mitigates tariff-induced losses in import-intensive Egypt (elasticity = +0.208) but yields only marginal relief in dollar-pegged Jordan (elasticity = +0.095). Global policy uncertainty exerts a comparable adverse effect, with a 1% rise in the World Uncertainty Index reducing exports by 15.6% (Egypt) and 17.2% (Jordan). The results underscore exchange rate flexibility as a pivotal resilience mechanism and highlight the acute vulnerability of small, open Arab economies to strategic trade weaponization, with aggregate 2025 export losses estimated at $610 million for Egypt and $1.03 billion for Jordan.

title: Do as We Say, Not as We Source: Global Anti-Discrimination Laws and U.S. Firms' Sourcing Decisions
affiliations: The University of Texas at El Paso and

detail.title: Do as We Say, Not as We Source: Global Anti-Discrimination Laws and U.S. Firms' Sourcing Decisions
detail.abstract: U.S. firms publicize commitments to non-discriminatory labor practices, but whether these commitments affect firm behavior is empirically untested: domestic federal enforcement has been static since the 1990s, and disclosures are endogenous. We exploit the staggered enactment of anti-discrimination laws (ADLs) across 78 countries from 1997 to 2017 to identify causal effects on foreign sourcing. A one-standard-deviation increase in a country's ADL count reduces sourcing by 19.5%, driven by reallocation toward less-regulated alternatives within existing supply networks. Firms continuing to source from treated countries incur higher costs and compressed margins. Collectively, these findings suggest that corporate non-discrimination commitments constitute cheap talk.

title: Hustle for Cash: Evidence from Nigeria's Naira Crunch

detail.title: Hustle for Cash: Evidence from Nigeria's Naira Crunch
detail.abstract: When Nigeria's central bank abruptly withdrew currency in late 2022 and capped cash withdrawals, the resulting shortage, the naira crunch, created a sharp, unanticipated cash supply shock. This paper exploits cross-state variation in pre-shock digital payment adoption, measured eleven days before the policy announcement, to estimate the real costs of the crunch and the insulating role of financial infrastructure. Using enterprise modules from the Nigeria Living Standards Phone Survey (1,842 household enterprises across three rounds), with the parallel-trends assumption validated through a 45month pre-shock nighttime-light panel covering all 774 Nigerian local government areas, enterprises in states one standard deviation above the pre-shock fintech mean were 1.7 percentage points more likely to remain in operation at peak crunch and 7.7 percentage points more likely to survive fourteen months later. Employment effects are also large: 0.29 additional enterprise workers per standard deviation of fintech at peak crunch. Effects are concentrated in rural and small enterprises. The results identify digital financial infrastructure as a macroeconomic stabiliser against cash supply disruptions, with implications for central bank currency operations in low-income economies.

title: Is Correlation Neglect Bad for Portfolio Diversification?
affiliations: University of Vienna - Department of Statistics and Operations Research

detail.title: Is Correlation Neglect Bad for Portfolio Diversification?
detail.abstract: While correlations play a central role in Markowitz portfolio selection, evidence shows that investors often neglect them, relying on simple heuristics rather than Pearson correlation. Standard theory suggests that incorporating correlations should improve performance, yet out-of-sample results frequently favor strategies that ignore them. This paper asks: Is correlation neglect always harmful, and which aspects of correlation truly matter? I propose a transformation that isolates the directional component of correlations and show that both fully ignoring and fully relying on correlation are suboptimal. Empirically, the directional component captures the most relevant information for diversification and improves portfolio performance. By distinguishing between the beneficial and irrelevant components of correlation coefficients, the paper provides a framework for constructing more robust portfolios.

title: Schema Before Capital in the NewVistas Constitutional Economy
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and Quaid-i-Azam University

detail.title: Schema Before Capital in the NewVistas Constitutional Economy
detail.abstract: This paper develops a formal institutional theory of Agency 19 within the NewVistas constitutional economy. The central problem addressed is how proposed productive stewardship can become admissible for market verification, underwriting, lease activation, credit-line use, consolidator closing, or purchase-transfer succession without collapsing into administrative planning, private capital allocation, or formula-based approval. The study models Agency 19 as a non-discretionary schema-completeness gate that operates before market and underwriting review. Methodologically, the Business Stewardship Plan is represented as a structured block vector, while Agency 19 is formalized as a noncompensatory admissibility operator requiring every field to be present, valid, versioned, priced, coherent, routed, privacy-bound, Life-Plan-consistent, settlement-correct, and formula-admissible. The findings show that incomplete plans, wealth-filtered entry requirements, raw-asset packages, fixed-multiple sale rules, incorrect community 10% fee ordering, false dashboard valuation claims, and succession defects cannot pass the origination gate. The paper's contribution is to identify Agency 19 as a distinctive institutional mechanism: it does not predict business success or allocate capital but prevents incomplete structure from becoming economic commitment. The conclusion is that NewVistas introduces a humane sequence in which life planning precedes business design, schema precedes capital, market evidence precedes underwriting, and residue remains protected from consumption or misclassification.

title: The Operator Theory of Automation: Technical Change as a Tra jectory in Function Space

detail.title: The Operator Theory of Automation: Technical Change as a Tra jectory in Function Space
detail.abstract: Neoclassical production theory describes input substitution through the marginal rate of technical substitution (MRTS), a ratio of partial derivatives evaluated along an isoquant of a xed production function. This paper shows that automation is not fully described by marginal substitution within a xed production function, and that the MRTS is the wrong instrument for measuring it. Production is modeled over a nite set of tasks, and automation is dened as an operator acting on the production function itself, deleting the labor coordinate of an automated task from the domain. Under this construction the marginal product of the eliminated labor is not small but undened, and the rate of substitution between labor and the automating capital is a type error rather than a number. The failure is independent of convention: retaining the coordinate as inert returns a degenerate zero, the menu convention places a nondierentiable kink exactly where the substitution occurs, and the value the classical limit assigns is arbitrary, adjustable to any number in [0, ∞] by a choice about a technology the event has removed. We develop the recursive structure that arises when the orchestration of automated tasks is itself automated, prove that surviving labor concentrates onto an essential node whose factor share decays geometrically in automation depth while leaving that node indispensable, characterize the investment frontier that governs which tasks are absorbed at a given cost of automation, show that acquiring the automation capability as an owned asset drives the marginal cost of further absorption down to the operating cost of the owned asset, and show that conditional on the documented decline in the price of xed capability the absorbed set grows on two margins while the labor share falls through three independent channels: depth, scale, and time. The unit of analysis ceases to be a point on a xed production surface and becomes a path through a space of production functions of changing dimension.

title: The Roles AI Is (and Should Be) Playing in Dispute Resolution On the Legitimacy of AI Legal Applications
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley - School of Law and Haifa University - Faculty of Law

detail.title: The Roles AI Is (and Should Be) Playing in Dispute Resolution On the Legitimacy of AI Legal Applications
detail.abstract: This chapter reviews the expanding roles of artificial intelligence, particularly large language models (LLMs), in dispute resolution and legal decision-making, examining both their current capabilities and the normative questions raised by their growing adoption. It synthesizes empirical research on public and professional perceptions of AI in courts and alternative dispute resolution, showing that acceptance of AI is highly context-dependent: users value AI for its accuracy, consistency, and efficiency, while continuing to prefer humans for empathy, discretion, and procedural fairness. The chapter argues that recent advances in LLMs are blurring this distinction, raising fundamental questions about the legitimacy of delegating increasingly sophisticated legal and dispute resolution functions to AI.

title: Exempt, Evade, Enforce: Unpacking Property Tax Dynamics in the Short-Term Rental Market

detail.title: Exempt, Evade, Enforce: Unpacking Property Tax Dynamics in the Short-Term Rental Market
detail.abstract: How does third-party reporting shape property tax compliance? Local governments depend on property taxes, yet compliance relies on self-reported property use with little verification. Short-term rental (STR) hosts exploit this gap by managing rental activity to retain owner-occupied exemptions. Using STR data from 2015-2024 in Florida, I apply a bunching estimator at the 30-day exemption threshold and exploit an enforcement shock to detect tax evasion. Bunching is negligible before the shock but grows substantially after, with hosts cutting bookings by more than 16 nights. Results show how lenient third-party reporting generates meaningful compliance gains in decentralized tax systems.

title: Writings on the Soil: Ascriptive Entitlements, Territorial Brokerage, and the Pseudo-Urban Breakdown of Malaysia's Dominant Party

detail.title: Writings on the Soil: Ascriptive Entitlements, Territorial Brokerage, and the Pseudo-Urban Breakdown of Malaysia's Dominant Party
detail.abstract: Whether urbanization threatens an electoral authoritarian regime depends on institutions the regime itself built: the state-made geography of ethnic groups, and the form of each group's distributive incorporation. A group incorporated through brokered exchange is tied to place: benefits flow through settlements and their brokers, and cities dissolve both. A group held by an ascriptive entitlement, i.e., benefits attached by law to membership, loses nothing when its members move. I test the argument in Malaysia, where land policy concentrated the Chinese minority near towns and rooted the Malay majority in the countryside, and the constitution assigned Malays the entitlement and the Chinese a place-bound, brokered margin. Using ecological inference, a settlement-level event study, and survey evidence across 1974-2018, I show that Chinese support collapsed where cities grew while Malay support held until an intra-elite rupture. Exclusion did not doom the regime; it decided which coalition could bring it down.

title: Handbook of Authoritarian Economic Analysis
affiliations: Peking University

detail.title: Handbook of Authoritarian Economic Analysis
detail.abstract:
China’s 25-year economic transition reveals structural deceleration driven by institutional rigidities and policy endogeneity rather than exogenous shocks. This paper synthesizes the framework g = G(I, D, P) , where long-run growth is shaped by institutional barriers (I ), distributional structures (D), and endogenous policy responses (P) constrained by the former two. 
The core “trilogy” — hukou-land dualism, regional convergence clubs, and high-frequency policy volatility — has locked the economy into a low-growth equilibrium, validating the author’s accurate 2012 forecast. Three diagnostic indices operationalize the analysis: the Rm index (monetary transmission insulation, exhaustion threshold 0.01), the Club40pct index (bottom-40% wage stagnation and macro-decoupling), and the J-index (real-time grassroots stress). 
Empirical results show that once these indices enter their respective “trap zones,” conventional counter-cyclical stimulus becomes macroeconomically sterile. Substantive “equal-rights” reforms in hukou portability, land-rights liberalization, and fiscal governance represent the binding constraint for restoring institutional efficiency and potential growth. The author’s work has paralleled and converged with Acemoglu and Robinson’s inclusive institutions thesis by offering a rigorous, China-specific model of endogenous deceleration grounded in empirical diagnostics.

title: Does Local Exposure to Climate Related Disasters Favour Sufficiency?
affiliations: Université de Bretagne Occidentale, University of Western Brittany (UBO) and Université de Caen - CREM UMR CNRS 6211

detail.title: Does Local Exposure to Climate Related Disasters Favour Sufficiency?
detail.abstract: This paper aims to assess if exposure to geographically proximate climate-related events fosters sufficiency behaviors. To support our findings, we provide empirical analyses (matching and mediation methods), using representative survey data from France. We consider 16 self-reported sustainable consumption choices from 1,519 respondents in 2024, matched with a range of climate-related events registered in the municipality of residence. In the first instance, our findings support the dual aspects of construal-level theory, showing that climate-related experiences can positively, negatively, or insignificantly affect sufficiency behaviors, depending on the climate risk considered and consumption practice. However, we also observe that perceived climate risks can have a greater influence on individual actions and beliefs than those directly observed in one's locality. Finally, we find that hypothetical distance and the belief that the responsibility to take action lies with others are the mediators that indirectly influence the probability that sufficiency-oriented behaviors will be adopted.

title: Selling Representation: The Effect of Out-of-District Donations on Candidate Positioning
affiliations: University of South Carolina

detail.title: Selling Representation: The Effect of Out-of-District Donations on Candidate Positioning
detail.abstract: The United States House of Representatives is intended to be the locally representative body of federal government. While only district residents are eligible to vote, residents of the entire country can donate to any candidate. This paper explores how much the pursuit of money from ideologically extreme donors explains candidates' deviations from representing their constituents. I estimate a structural model of a candidate's ideology choice in which candidates care about winning, which tends to pull them to the ideological center, and fundraising, which tends to pull them to the ideological extremes. A counterfactual prohibition on out-of-district giving would achieve two-fifths of the reduction in polarization that would arise if candidates' positions maximized their win probability. Moreover, a third of the polarization reduction could be achieved without a ban on out-of-district giving, but rather, via the endogenous reduction in out-of-district giving that would arise if districts were drawn to reflect statewide preferences.

title: Soil Organic Carbon Loss Under Climate Change in a Chilean Mediterranean Dryland: Warming Versus Persistent Drought
affiliations: University of Concepción - Escuela de Administración y Negocios

detail.title: Soil Organic Carbon Loss Under Climate Change in a Chilean Mediterranean Dryland: Warming Versus Persistent Drought
detail.abstract: Soil organic carbon (SOC) in Mediterranean drylands is highly vulnerable to climate change, yet no process-based SOC assessment exists for Chile’s secano interior, a ∼2 million-hectare rain-fed cropland region gripped since 2010 by the most severe drought in roughly a millennium. Using the RothC-26.3 model, calibrated to regional baseline stocks and driven by station-corrected historical weather and five-model NEX-GDDP CMIP6 projections, we simulated topsoil (0–30cm) SOC from 1985 to 2100 at two sites spanning the region’s rainfall and soil-carbon gradient, under three climate fu tures (SSP2-4.5, SSP5-8.5, and a persistent-drought scenario) and three managements (conventional tillage, no-tillage with residue retention, and residue burning), and de composed the projected loss into warming and drying contributions. The megadrought, with rainfall deficits of 32–33%, had already drawn model-inferred topsoil carbon down by about 8% by 2024. SOC declined further under every climate future, by 4–17% over 2025–2100, with SSP5-8.5 the most damaging. Attribution revealed two regimes: under the climate-model scenarios warming was the leading driver of loss (48–68% of the climate-driven change), whereas reduced rainfall dominated (70–77%) only if the megadrought persists. No-tillage with residue retention offset 22–73% of the high emission loss and reversed it to a net gain under moderate warming, but in no case cancelled it; residue burning was the most damaging practice under every scenario. These are the first process-based SOC trajectories for Mediterranean Chile and provide a quantitative, regionally calibrated basis for conservation policy and further mecha nistic study.

reference: Herrera Anchustegui, I. Pereira, E.G., Wifa, E. and Taylor, M., 2025. On the future of offshore energy. In Offshore energy law: challenges and opportunities for renewables and hydrocarbons (pp. 387-404). Hart Publishing.
title: Chapter 18: On the Future of Offshore Energy
affiliations: University of Bergen, Faculty of Law, Macquarie University - Macquarie Law School (Sydney, Australia), affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Chapter 18: On the Future of Offshore Energy

declarations.funderStatement: The research for this chapter has benefited from the generous funding granted by the Research Council of Norway to the research projects: Norwegian Centre for Hydrogen Research—HyValue (Project: 333151); and ImpactWind Sørvest (Project: 332034), and the Transforming Energy Markets Research Centre, Macquarie University. All websites were last accessed on 10 October 2024.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Herrera Anchustegui, I. Pereira, E.G., Wifa, E. and Taylor, M., 2025. On the future of offshore energy. In Offshore energy law: challenges and opportunities for renewables and hydrocarbons (pp. 387-404). Hart Publishing.

detail.abstract: This chapter explores the future direction of offshore energy law and governance in the context of the energy transition, expanding marine industrial activity, and increasing climate-related regulatory pressures. Drawing on the contributions to Offshore Energy Law, it identifies key legal and policy challenges across environmental governance, community participation, financing, and infrastructure development. The analysis highlights emerging issues relating to marine spatial planning, offshore activities beyond national jurisdiction, Indigenous and community rights, local content policies, financing mechanisms, and integrated energy projects. It argues that the growing interdependence of offshore energy systems challenges sector-specific regulatory models and requires more integrated governance approaches. The chapter concludes by outlining a research agenda centred on energy justice, environmental stewardship, infrastructure coordination, and climate responsibility as defining themes for the next generation of offshore energy regulation

title: Courts of Tomorrow: Evidence from a Nationwide Rollout of Generative AI
affiliations: New Economic School (NES), ETH Zürich and ETH Zürich

detail.title: Courts of Tomorrow: Evidence from a Nationwide Rollout of Generative AI
detail.abstract: We present the first large-scale field experiment evaluating the integration of generative AI into a national justice system. In partnership with Pakistan’s judiciary, we built \textit{JudgeGPT}, a custom generative AI assistant designed for Pakistan’s trial courts, and randomized 1,559 judges serving across 118 courts into one of three arms: (i) access to the assistant with targeted training tailored to its use; (ii) access to AI with generic training on technology and law; and (iii) generic training without access to AI. Judges who received AI access together with targeted training on the use of the tool were more likely to adopt it, use it more intensively, and continue using it over time. Their attitudes toward AI also shift: they expect the tool and the targeted training to increase their productivity. Administrative records move in the same direction: districts with greater exposure to treated judges resolve more cases. At median-district exposure, introducing AI with targeted training corresponds to 1,848 additional cases resolved per year, a 6.3 percent increase over the mean. This increase does not appear to come at the expense of reduced quality, as measured by case appeals (which slightly decline) or text-based measures of judicial writing (which slightly improve). Chat-log-based usage patterns suggest that judges use AI mainly to clarify legal concepts and support drafting. Targeted training appears to shift use toward tasks where language models are likely to be more useful, such as text improvement, and away from more open-ended legal queries where responses are more costly to verify. Overall, the results suggest that generative AI can raise public-sector productivity, but that these gains may depend on targeted training that directs use toward tasks for which the tool is better suited.

title: Decomposing Price Chart Signals in Return Prediction
affiliations: , Aarhus University and Aarhus University - Department of Economics and Business Economics

detail.title: Decomposing Price Chart Signals in Return Prediction
detail.abstract: Image models trained on stock charts predict returns out of sample, though a chart adds no information beyond the OHLCV data it renders. We decompose the image model's advantage over tabular benchmarks from the same daily window into three sources: function-class capacity, chart-specific encoding, and how each model smooths noisy returns. Capacity contributes little. Under a distillation accounting, roughly 60% of the apparent gap is tied to learning from noisy realized returns rather than chart-specific content. The residual localizes to recent bars, intraday extremes, and temporal order, and is largely recoverable with explicit predictors.

title: Discussion of "Auditing Smart Contracts:" Assurance in the World of Decentralized Finance
affiliations: University of Toronto

detail.title: Discussion of "Auditing Smart Contracts:" Assurance in the World of Decentralized Finance

declarations.funderStatement: Rotman Finhub in Financial Innovation

detail.abstract: Smart contracts implement financial logic on public blockchains, and external code audits are a primary means of providing assurance about their security. This paper discusses Landsman, Lyandres, Maydew, Rabetti, and Zhang (Journal of Accounting and Economics, forthcoming), who describe and analyze the market for smart contract audits. I provide a brief primer on blockchains and smart contracts, explain what distinguishes blockchainbased finance from traditional finance, outline why no audit can guarantee security in an open, permissionless environment, and discuss how Landsman et al.s findings relate to financial auditing. A central result in their paper is that pre-launch audits do not predict fewer breaches, which is noteworthy and consistent with the view that a smart contract audit, like a financial audit, is a snapshot, not a shield. Beyond the conceptual and methodological parallels between smart contract and financial audits, two distinctive features merit the attention of accounting scholars: open code forking, which creates networks of common-code exposure and correlated systemic risk, and bug bounty programs, which provide a crowdsourced and potentially continuous form of assurance.

title: Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) and Financial Fragility within a Capacity-constrained Credit Policy

detail.title: Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) and Financial Fragility within a Capacity-constrained Credit Policy
detail.abstract: The financial stability implications of a retail CBDC depend on how it is integrated into the central bank's crisis-response framework. This paper studies CBDC-based credit policy in a dynamic macro-banking model with anticipated runs. The key friction is the capacity-constrained credit policy: following an adverse productivity shock, the central bank may be unable to extend the necessary emergency lending immediately, restoring intervention only gradually. The model shows that this constraint can make self-fulfilling runs feasible because runnable deposit claims remain large relative to the fire-sale value of bank assets. However, the numerical exercise shows that an economy with a capacity-constrained credit policy still improves resilience relative to an economy without central bank lending. Finally, the model is extended by introducing central bank reserves as a safe asset held by banks. By adding a safe payoff to run-state resources, reserves raise depositor recovery and can eliminate the run equilibrium, although they may shift bank portfolios away from productive capital.

title: The K-Factor Efficient Frontier
affiliations: Tulane University

detail.title: The K-Factor Efficient Frontier
detail.abstract: Empirical asset pricing has long sought parsimonious factor models for the cross-section. I study the maximum efficiency, in squared Sharpe ratio, that any such model can attain via the K-factor efficient frontier. I show that a tractable, cardinality constrained regression with a natural economic interpretation traces the frontier. The lasso does not, because the l1 penalty selects factors on their alphas, not their contributions to the frontier's squared Sharpe ratio. A 15-factor cardinality-constrained portfolio attains an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of 3.14, which matches the Sharpe ratio of a 158-factor dense benchmark portfolio. A 15-factor lasso portfolio reaches 2.74.

title: Synthetic Risk Transfer in Indian Banking: An Unaddressed Capital Optimisation Gap
affiliations: ICFAI Business School (IBS) Hyderabad, India

detail.title: Synthetic Risk Transfer in Indian Banking: An Unaddressed Capital Optimisation Gap

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. This research was conducted independently and received no funding from any financial institution, corporation, or regulatory body. The author has no financial relationship with any of the banks or institutions referenced in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This research did not involve human subjects, clinical trials, animal studies, or the collection of personal data. All data used in this paper were sourced from publicly available regulatory documents, bank annual reports, and industry publications. No ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted independently by the author as part of self-initiated academic research.

detail.abstract: Synthetic risk transfer (SRT) is a structured finance technique through which banks transfer the credit risk of a reference loan portfolio to institutional investors while retaining the underlying assets on balance sheet. The global SRT market exceeds $30 billion in annual issuance, with over 650 transactions executed by 51 banks across Europe, the United States, and emerging markets since 2016. As of this writing, no synthetic risk transfer transaction has been publicly documented in India. This paper examines whether this absence reflects a genuine lack of economic rationale or an unaddressed market gap. Using publicly disclosed Basel III Pillar 3 data from India's largest private sector banks, we estimate the regulatory capital cost embedded in off-balance-sheet financial guarantee portfolios and find it to be substantial. We document five structural barriers that explain the absence of an Indian SRT market, none of which appear permanent, and propose a regulatory and transactional pathway through which a first transaction could be executed. We conclude that the absence of an Indian SRT market is best explained as a coordination failure among capable parties rather than an absence of economic incentive.

title: Carbon Policy and Market-Based Inflation Expectations
affiliations: University of Orleans, Laboratoire d'économie d'Orléans, Students and Banque de France

detail.title: Carbon Policy and Market-Based Inflation Expectations
detail.abstract: Does the environmental transition shape market-based inflation expectations? Using a high-frequency event study on euro-area inflation-linked swap rates over 2021-2025, we show that EU ETS2 and ETS1 legislative and regulatory events significantly raise inflation compensation, especially at long-run maturities, while short-term expectations remain unaffected. This effect is driven by events that structurally alter the functioning of the EU carbon market, rather than by short-lived policy adjustments. These results suggest that financial markets interpret major carbon-policy events as signals of persistent inflationary pressures stemming from the green transition.

title: Better Together? Female Instructors, Female Advisors, and Women's Persistence in Economics
affiliations: University of Wisconsin - La Crosse, University of Wisconsin-La Crosse, University of Wisconsin - La Crosse, University of Wisconsin-La Crosse and University of Wisconsin-La Crosse

detail.title: Better Together? Female Instructors, Female Advisors, and Women's Persistence in Economics

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We have no relevant or material financial interests related to the research described in this paper and received no funding to support it.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The University of Wisconsin–La Crosse Institutional Review Board reviewed and approved this research under expedited procedures (Protocol ID IRB 25-MEN-179). The analysis uses deidentified administrative records supplied by the university; no direct interaction with human subjects occurred, and all procedures met applicable ethical standards for research involving human subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: Female instructors and female advisors each matter for women's persistence in economics. We ask whether the two work better together than apart and whether this is specific to women. Using administrative records from a broad-access public university, we combine quasi-random instructor assignment with plausibly exogenous advisor assignment. Among women, the share taking an advanced economics course rises from 14 to 23 percent when both are female, more than either alone suggests, while men show no comparable pattern. Major completion moves in the same direction, although the evidence is more suggestive. The effect of a female instructor may depend on the advising that students receive.

title: Does Formalisation Matter for Informal Sector Enterprises? Evidence From a Primary Firm Survey in Assam, India
affiliations: Dibrugarh University

detail.title: Does Formalisation Matter for Informal Sector Enterprises? Evidence From a Primary Firm Survey in Assam, India

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest. Single Author
declarations.ethicsApproval: Does not arise
declarations.funderStatement: Nil

detail.abstract: This paper examines the effect of levels of formality on the performance of informal manufacturing firms. Research on the benefits of formalization on the microenterprises is scarcer, particularly in India, a country with a large informal sector. We follow prior works to argue that informal firms function at different levels of informality. Our article tries to assess the effect of the levels of formality on the firm level outcomes. It uses primary data from a survey of 205 informal manufacturing enterprises from the Indian state of Assam. Tools employed in our study include ordinary least squares (OLS) regression, and a multinomial logit regression. Findings reveal that effect of formality differs across the measures of firm performance. A higher level of formality is found to have a positive relationship with labour productivity, and growth of the enterprises, but its effect is found weak on the mixed income accruing to entrepreneur's household.

reference: Herrera Anchustegui, I. and Eskeland, G. (2025) ‘Should Owners of Carbon-Intensive Assets Be Compensated if Required to Cease Operation Due to the Energy Transition?’, in L. Reins and A. detail.abstract: This chapter examines whether owners of carbon-intensive assets should be compensated when climate policies require the premature cessation of operations. Drawing on legal and economic analysis, it explores the tension between the protection of property and contractual rights, on the one hand, and the state's authority to pursue climate mitigation measures in the public interest, on the other. The chapter reviews constitutional principles, human rights law, investment law, and selected European case law, including disputes concerning coal-fired power plants in Germany and the Netherlands. It argues that compensation may be justified when government action is discriminatory, disproportionate, or undermines legitimate expectations, particularly where closures are abrupt and targeted. Equally, compensation may be unwarranted where climate measures are foreseeable, generally applicable, and adopted through lawful regulatory processes. The analysis suggests that the key determinants are not the environmental character of the measure itself, but its universality, predictability, and proportionality. These factors are likely to shape future disputes arising from the transition to a low-carbon economy

detail.abstract: This report analyzes five machine-generated model AI policies for law school coursework and examinations, produced by Harvey AI, Grok, Claude, Gemini, and ChatGPT in response to a prompt asking each system to construct a policy from the standpoint of computational machine intelligence, and compares them against Backer's related empirical study of twelve U.S. law school AI policies, "Structure, Opacity, and Convergence". The analysis summarizes each system's reasoning and resulting policy text, compares their structural choices along default polarity, drafting style, and autonomy architecture, and categorizes the five outputs by these dimensions. It gives particular attention to the functional divergence between Gemini's tool-based tiering (classifying software by computational architecture) and ChatGPT's task-based categorization (classifying assignments by information dependence), and assesses the practical feasibility of the versioning and archiving practices several systems propose. The analysis further considers, against the underlying Report's documented findings on axis independence, institutional opacity, template convergence, and faculty autonomy, the extent to which these machine-generated models affect the scope of human agency in law and their consequential implications for law's character as a human inter-operative system-finding that several systems' proceduralized verification requirements shift the evidentiary basis of agency toward documentation compliance, and that much of the systems' apparent computational originality derives from pre-existing human regulatory-design scholarship. Finally, the report documents a self-audit correcting citation-indexing errors and a mischaracterization suggesting Gemini underwent a shown revision process comparable to Harvey's and ChatGPT's, which the retrieved text does not support. Divided into an introduction and ten (10 substantive parts, this document captures a multi-stage experiment by Professor Larry Catá Backer, who asked five leading AI systems-Harvey AI, Grok, Claude, Gemini, and ChatGPT-to each construct, from "the basis of computational machine intelligence" and without endorsing any human position, a model AI policy for law school coursework and exams, and then pushed each system with a follow-up challenge to expose the value judgments hidden in its own language.

detail.title: Asymmetric Analysis of Okun's Law: The Case for Turkey
detail.abstract: This paper revisits Okun's law under an asymmetric approach for Turkey applying structural threshold regression model that allows for endogeneity of the threshold variable that separates the dataset into low and high regime periods according to economic growth. Moreover, the theory is investigated taking subcategories of unemployment rate into account, such as age, education and gender. Empirical findings suggest that only the overall unemployment rate and female unemployment rate reflect significantly negative impacts in both periods. During deep recessions, unemployment rates are more responsive to economic growth.

title: The Gate and the Playground: Age Attestation, Exclusion, and the Architecture of Verified Peer Space

detail.title: The Gate and the Playground: Age Attestation, Exclusion, and the Architecture of Verified Peer Space

detail.abstract: The age assurance debate has settled into a standoff between child safety and privacy in which each side concedes the other has a real interest and neither produces an architecture that serves both. This paper argues that the framing is wrong. The binding constraint on age assurance is neither safety nor privacy. It is exclusion, and exclusion is a distribution problem rather than a cryptographic one. The cryptography required to prove that a person is over a given age without disclosing the person's name, birthday, face, or any other attribute has existed since 1983, and the hardware required to bind a credential to the human presenting it is a deployed W3C standard. What does not exist is a credential that reaches everyone. Every scheme now on the table requires the subject to apply, to pay, to travel, to produce documents, or to own a device manufactured by one of the two companies the scheme is meant to regulate, and each of those requirements falls on the same populations: the poor, the undocumented, and the disabled. This paper proposes the distributive inversion. A boolean age predicate, blind signed by the issuing state, delivered on free standalone hardware, issued at birth alongside the identifiers a government already assigns, and entitled rather than applied for. It further argues that age assurance requires two credentials and not one, because a binary attestation that a holder is over eighteen forces responsible guardians to make platforms blind to the children they are trying to protect, and that the correct deliverable of the architecture is composition rather than exclusion: a space in which every occupant is a verified peer, every occupant's guardian has consented, and intensive supervision therefore raises no adult privacy objection because there is no adult inside to raise one. It argues that supervision is not an addition to the gate but the only mechanism that detects a compromised credential, which converts the rule against treating a gate as a discharge from a policy preference into an architectural necessity. It rejects the zero retention instinct on the ground that a child groomed at thirteen and disclosing at sixteen needs the record to exist, and proposes instead that the objection to retention was never duration but custody and purpose, resolved by escrow. The paper closes by identifying what the architecture does not solve, including the guardian who is himself the threat, the impossibility of binding an infant, the severing of relationships at band boundaries, and the bystander, who never approaches a gate at all and for whom no credential architecture can substitute for a rule keyed to the data subject.

title: Urban-Rural Integration and Industrial Structural Transformation: Evidence from a Comprehensive Panel Analysis of Chinese Provinces

detail.title: Urban-Rural Integration and Industrial Structural Transformation: Evidence from a Comprehensive Panel Analysis of Chinese Provinces
detail.abstract: Urban-rural integration has become an important institutional approach to easing structural distortions and promoting balanced development, yet its implications for industrial transformation remain insufficiently understood. Drawing on provincial panel data for China, this study investigates whether and how urban-rural integration affects both the upgrading and rationalization of the industrial structure. An integrated empirical framework is employed, combining two-way fixed-effects estimation, policy evaluation, heterogeneity analysis, mediation modeling, and threshold testing. The results show that a higher level of urban-rural integration is significantly associated with improvements in both industrial upgrading and structural rationalization, indicating that spatial and institutional integration can promote a more advanced and more efficiently coordinated industrial system. Reform-oriented integration policies further reinforce these effects. At the same time, the impact of integration is heterogeneous across regions, with stronger effects observed in non-resource-oriented provinces and in regions with higher innovation capacity. The development of technology markets functions as an important transmission mechanism linking integration to structural transformation. The analysis also suggests that the structural effects of urban-rural integration are influenced by the broader distributional context of development, and tend to be stronger when the benefits of economic development are shared more evenly between urban and rural residents. These findings underscore the importance of institutional integration, market development, and inclusive development in facilitating structural transformation, while offering policy insights for economies seeking to reduce urban-rural segmentation and foster high-quality industrial development.

title: Patriarchal Systems and the Reproduction of Gender Inequality in South Asia: A Structural Analysis of Child Marriage, Education, and Social Norms
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Patriarchal Systems and the Reproduction of Gender Inequality in South Asia: A Structural Analysis of Child Marriage, Education, and Social Norms
detail.abstract: Gender inequality in South Asia remains a persistent social issue despite improvements in education, legal frameworks, and development indicators. This paper examines how patriarchal systems contribute to the continuation of gender inequality through interconnected structures, with a particular focus on child marriage, education, and social norms. Using a qualitative secondary research approach, this study analyzes feminist theory, academic research, and reports from international organizations to explore how family structures, cultural expectations, economic systems, and institutional practices shape the experiences of girls and women. Drawing on Sylvia Walby's theory of patriarchy and Kalwant Bhopal's intersectional perspective, this paper argues that gender inequality is not produced by a single factor but through overlapping systems that reinforce unequal gender relations. The analysis demonstrates that child marriage is sustained through social expectations surrounding family honor, sexuality, economic insecurity, and women's traditional roles. Furthermore, educational progress alone does not eliminate inequality when broader social and economic structures continue to restrict female autonomy. The study concludes that addressing gender inequality requires structural transformation rather than isolated interventions, as lasting change depends on challenging the systems that define girls' opportunities and social value.

title: Planning Parkour Parks as Public Physical Activity Environments in Finland: Practitioner Expertise and Participation
affiliations: University of Helsinki, Helsinki University and

detail.title: Planning Parkour Parks as Public Physical Activity Environments in Finland: Practitioner Expertise and Participation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Parkour parks translate the creative use of non-dedicated urban environments into purposebuilt physical activity environments. This article examines that transformation through four Finnish cases: Valkola in Laukaa, Kaleva Central Park in Tampere, Lippumäki in Kuopio, and Namika Areena in Helsinki. The study draws on interviews with four key planning and implementation actors and six parkour practitioner experts, supported by site photographs and contextual documents. The analysis compared project pathways, actor roles, practitioner expertise, and material design. The findings show that the parks were justified mainly through local demand, children's and young people's activity, neighbourhood recreation, and sport service provision. Practitioner expertise had the strongest influence when it entered early enough to shape equipment selection, layout, or site-specific design. Practitioner experts considered all four parks usable for some forms of movement but raised concerns about modular repetition, obstacle spacing, surface materials, slipperiness, limited run-up or landing space, and the capacity of standardized parks to support diverse parkour styles. The article argues that parkour parks should be understood not only as sport facilities but as public physical activity environments whose usability depends on translating embodied movement expertise into material design. It contributes to public space scholarship by showing how practice-based expertise shapes specialized recreational environments through its timing and role in planning and procurement.

title: Existence and Convergence of Discrete-Time Kyle Models with Multiple Insiders
affiliations: Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology (UNIST) and Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey

detail.title: Existence and Convergence of Discrete-Time Kyle Models with Multiple Insiders
detail.abstract: Foster and Viswanathan (1996) extend the discrete-time setting of Kyle (1985) to multiple informed traders who have partial information about the stock's terminal dividend. We resolve two long-standing open problems in this literature. First, we prove that an equilibrium exists in the setting of Foster and Viswanathan (1996). Second, as the number of trading times goes to infinity, we prove that the discrete-time equilibrium converges to the continuous-time equilibrium already proven to exist in Back, Cao, and Willard (2000).

detail.abstract: This study explored India’s multilateral intra-industry trade trends, noting a substantial rise, especially since 2000s. A focused examination within specific industries identifies electronic and transportation commodity groups as the principal drivers of this escalating trend. The analysis centered on factors influencing India’s intra-industry trade (IIT), emphasizing on revealed comparative advantage (RCA) and an outward-oriented trade policy. The RCA-IIT relationship unveils an inverted U-shaped curve. Significantly, a positive relationship emerges between IIT and an outward-oriented trade policy, highlighting the impact of trade liberalization on enhancing IIT. These findings hold crucial policy implications, indicating the role of trade liberalization initiatives in increasing IIT in India.

title: How Do Ecological Restoration Programs Shape Grain Production? Evidence from China's Three-North Shelter Forest Program
affiliations: Beijing Forestry University, Beijing Forestry University and Beijing Forestry University

detail.title: How Do Ecological Restoration Programs Shape Grain Production? Evidence from China's Three-North Shelter Forest Program
detail.abstract: Balancing ecological restoration and grain production is a core challenge for land management in arid and semi-arid regions. Large-scale ecological engineering programs are often assumed to constrain agricultural output through land-use competition, yet rigorous causal evidence on their long-term effects and underlying mechanisms remains scarce. This study investigates whether and how China's Three-North Shelter Forest Program (TNSFP) affects grain production. Guided by the social-ecological systems framework and ecosystem services theory, we hypothesize that large-scale ecological restoration can enhance agricultural output through improvements in ecosystem services rather than crowding out cropland. Using county-level panel data from China covering 2000-2022, we estimate the causal impact of TNSFP on grain production employing a two-way fixed effects model, complemented by the Callaway and Sant'Anna difference-indifferences approach (CSDID), event-study analysis, placebo tests, and multiple robustness checks. Grain production data are combined with satellite-derived vegetation indices, air quality indicators, and ecosystem quality measures to identify mechanism pathways. The results show that TNSFP significantly increases county-level grain production, with baseline estimates indicating an average rise of approximately 3.4 units and larger effects after controlling for agricultural inputs, climate, and socioeconomic conditions. CSDID estimates confirm robust positive effects,. Event-study results reveal negligible pre-treatment trends and gradually accumulating post-treatment effects. Mechanism analysis demonstrates that improved vegetation cover, enhanced air quality, and overall ecosystem quality jointly promote grain production, with ecosystem quality playing a dominant role. Significant regional and land endowment heterogeneity is observed, with stronger effects in cropland-abundant counties and limited impacts in Northwest China. These findings provide new causal evidence that ecological restoration can generate synergistic benefits for land restoration and food production, offering important implications for sustainable land management in dryland regions.

title: "Sanctions and the Uneven Reorganisation of Labour Regimes in Iran"
affiliations: State University of New York (SUNY) - Stony Brook, Students

detail.title: "Sanctions and the Uneven Reorganisation of Labour Regimes in Iran"

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.

detail.abstract: In what ways do sanctions transform labour regimes within sanctioned economies? Existing research has shown that sanctions generate macroeconomic disruption, including inflation, fiscal pressure, currency instability, welfare erosion, and employment loss. Less attention has been given to how these pressures are translated into labour control and social reproduction. This article develops a labour-regime approach to sanctions by analysing them as a restriction on the monetary, material, and infrastructural circulation required for industrial accumulation. Drawing on a comparative process tracing across five Iranian industrial sites, it argues that sanctions reorganise labour through uneven forms of incorporation rather than a uniform labour-market shock. In strategic sectors, state support helps sustain production, while workers are incorporated through subcontracting, segmented benefits and weakened claims on the main employer. In declining sectors, workers are attached to eroded production through wage arrears, legal claims, and demands for state intervention. The article contributes to labour-regime theory by showing how geopolitical coercion is absorbed into industrial organisation through protected production, managed decline, and the displacement of reproductive costs onto workers and households.

title: When Prices Cannot Fall: Asymmetric Price Limits and the Information Content of Trading Volume
affiliations: and Universiti Malaysia Terengganu (UMT)

detail.title: When Prices Cannot Fall: Asymmetric Price Limits and the Information Content of Trading Volume
detail.abstract: Between 20 July 2020 and 31 May 2021, Bursa Malaysia halved the daily limit on how far every stock could fall while leaving the limit on gains untouched. Regime changes studied to date have moved both limits together or applied only to distressed firms; this one moved one side of an entire market for ten months and then moved it back. We use the episode, together with the rule driven cross section of band widths that Malaysia's sen denominated limits create, to measure how constraints on price discovery reshape the information in trading volume. In a survivorship free panel of 902 firms over 2016 to 2025, surprise volume forecasts next day volatility twice as strongly as expected volume, and this informativeness rises with the mechanical tightness of a firm's band even in the ordinary regime. Inside the window, floor touches multiply nearly forty-fold and the falling day volume signal triples. Exposure based difference in differences separates rule from episode: the informativeness surge is market wide, not concentrated in the firms the new floor could reach, while the mechanical costs, more frequent hits and elevated next day volatility, land on exactly those firms. In the upper tail of the volatility distribution, where risk models are judged, surprise volume speaks nearly four times as loudly as in calm states while predictable volume inverts into a dampener. Volume is a policy contingent signal. Regulators who compress price discovery should expect information to migrate into trading activity, and risk systems should read it there.

title: Agentic AI, Price Discovery, and Endogenous Human Innovation in Finance
affiliations: HEC Montreal

detail.title: Agentic AI, Price Discovery, and Endogenous Human Innovation in Finance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A

detail.abstract: Research in intelligent finance shows that agentic AI improves portfolio construction, default prediction, fraud detection, and network-risk identification by separating payoff-relevant signal from noisy data. This article models the economic and social impact of that improvement once the signal enters human decision-making and market prices. Let θₜ denote the pre-decision state, sₖ,ₜ an increasingly precise agentic signal, and pₖ,ₜ=E[vₜ|Fᵐₜ,sₖ,ₜ,oₜ] a price formed from public information, the agentic signal, and order flow. Blackwell improvement lowers current-state pricing error and can reduce informational asymmetry, improve allocation, and widen access to information. The same gain expands human search. Economic agents update beliefs, revise timing, recombine instruments, and create actions absent from the original model; these responses form part of θₜ₊₁. A projection result establishes improved price informativeness for the current state. A second result shows that information-induced innovation can coexist with that improvement while preventing mean-square convergence of successor state to a deterministic fixed point. Nonstationarity is not evidence that agentic AI failed. It may be the measurable consequence of information provision and human innovation. Economic and social impact should be evaluated through price discovery, decision quality, endogenous option creation, distribution, and dynamic welfare.

title: "Sanctions, Value-Chain Rupture, and the Recomposition of Labour Bargaining Power in Iran"
affiliations: State University of New York (SUNY) - Stony Brook, Students

detail.title: "Sanctions, Value-Chain Rupture, and the Recomposition of Labour Bargaining Power in Iran"

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This research involved no human subjects or participants. The research is mainly done by document and secondary analysis.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract: This article argues that economic sanctions recompose labour bargaining power in Iran by producing value-chain rupture, understood as sanctions-driven disruption of settlement and procurement that makes production and revenue realisation intermittent and uncertain. Sanctions constrain payment, foreign-exchange access, and compliance-dependent trade infrastructures, and firms respond through wage delay, selective operation, and employment fragmentation. The article analyses these dynamics through three levers of labour power, marketplace, workplace, and associational, by tracing how sanctions alter the conditions under which exit, disruption, and organisation translate into outcomes. Drawing on a sectoral comparison of HEPCO in importexposed manufacturing and Campaign 1400 in the energy sector, the analysis shows how uneven exposure and buffering capacity generate distinct bargaining environments. In import-dependent manufacturing, procurement ruptures and liquidity crises compress outside options and reduce the efficacy of work stoppage, often rerouting claims into state-mediated channels. In strategic energy nodes, coordinated disruption can impose costs more directly, but fireability, settlement constraints, and fragmented employment limit gains and shorten organisational time horizons. The article specifies how uneven value-chain rupture shapes bargaining outcomes and constrains the durability of collective organisation in sanctioned economies.

title: The Microstructure of European Electricity Markets: A Review of Nord Pool, EPEX SPOT, XBID/SIDC, and the Consolidated Order Book
affiliations: Imperial College London - Department of Mathematics, Imperial College London and Imperial College London

detail.title: The Microstructure of European Electricity Markets: A Review of Nord Pool, EPEX SPOT, XBID/SIDC, and the Consolidated Order Book
detail.abstract: Short-term electricity markets in Europe have evolved from national pools into a tightly coupled, pan-European market architecture comprising a single day-ahead coupling (SDAC), a single intraday coupling (SIDC, formerly the XBID project) built around a consolidated shared order book, complementary intraday auctions (IDAs), and harmonised balancing platforms. This review surveys the institutional design and the market microstructure of these markets, with particular attention to Nord Pool, EPEX SPOT, the XBID/SIDC continuous trading solution, and the economics of order-book consolidation across exchanges and borders. We cover the mechanics of the day-ahead auction and the EUPHEMIA algorithm, the contract and order-type taxonomy of the continuous intraday market, gate-closure conventions, tick sizes and price bounds, and the transition to fifteen-minute market time units completed in 2025. We then review the empirical microstructure literature: liquidity and bid-ask spread dynamics, the concentration of trading activity near gate closure, fundamental price formation, self-exciting order-flow models based on Hawkes processes, market impact and liquidity costs, very-short-term price forecasting, and optimal trading and reinforcement-learning approaches. We discuss the interaction between intraday trading and imbalance settlement, the continuous-versusauction market-design debate, competition among nominated electricity market operators sharing a single order book, and open research problems including the microstructure of intraday auctions, flow-based intraday capacity allocation, and the latency arms race in algorithmic power trading.

title: A Different Perspective on the Keynes Model: Is Keynes a Demand-Side Economist?
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: A Different Perspective on the Keynes Model: Is Keynes a Demand-Side Economist?
detail.abstract: Since the publication of The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money, Keynes has remained one of the most influential figures in modern economics. Keynesian economics, through its various theoretical adaptations, continues to serve as a fundamental reference framework for macroeconomic policy design and analysis in both developed and developing countries. This paper challenges the widely accepted view in contemporary macroeconomics that Keynes was a demand-side economist. Drawing on the General Theory, together with the relevant literature, we argue that I ≡ Sbased models are insufficient to represent the supply-side effects of investment and contain analytical and mathematical inconsistencies. To address these limitations, we develop a new theoretical macroeconomic model within the aggregate supply-aggregate demand (AS-AD) framework that incorporates the effects of investment expenditures on both aggregate demand and aggregate supply, thereby offering an alternative to conventional one-sided approaches. We also develop a new microeconomic model within the framework of perfectly competitive supply-demand analysis that incorporates the demand effects arising from changes in the number of firms. Furthermore, building on the interaction between supply and demand-a methodological approach adopted by Keynes himselfwe propose an integrated graphical representation of Keynes's theory of employment within the AS-AD framework. Taken together, the analytical results obtained from the original models and representations developed in this study, together with the comparisons with the existing literature and the examination of Keynes's original text, suggest that Keynes's analytical framework incorporates a significant supply-side dimension that is compatible with the basic logic of Say's Law and therefore cannot be adequately characterized as an exclusively demand-side approach.

title: Are LLMs Reliable Coders of Communication Content in Economic Experiments?
affiliations: , Division of Social Science & Center for Behavioral Institutional Design, NYU Abu Dha and New York University of Abu Dhabi

detail.title: Are LLMs Reliable Coders of Communication Content in Economic Experiments?
detail.abstract: Analysis of free-form communication from experiments has largely relied on manual coding by research assistants (RAs), a costly and time-consuming process. We outline an easily implemented method for coding communication data using large language models (LLMs) and propose a novel standard for evaluating the performance of LLM-based coding ("reliability"). Using data from three published articles, we find that LLM-based coding meets our two reliability conditions: (1) differences between LLM-based and RA-based coding are no larger than differences between the RA-based and original coding and (2) the LLM-based coding largely replicates qualitative conclusions from the original papers. That said, there are cases where the LLM-based coding agrees poorly with the RA-based coding or fails to replicate statistical results from the original papers. We demonstrate that these problems can be ameliorated with better prompt design. We conclude that use of LLMs can reduce research costs and time without sacrificing reliability, making content analysis a more accessible tool for experimental economists. However, only with a combination of test coding by RAs and prompt design by researchers can we avoid significant problems with LLM-based coding, highlighting the continued importance of human input.
